docs.title: Welcome to Bonfire
docs.text: Bonfire provides CodeIgniter 4 applications with powerful tools, and a ready-to-integrate admin area, to help you build robust applications faster. It does not aim to be a full CMS, but rather a framework to help you build your own web application or internal tools.

docs.title: Important features
docs.text:
• Powerful and flexible user authentication system, with either password or personal access tokens
  • Simple theme system with reusable component system
  • Admin area
  • Easily expandable users
  • Possibility to easily integrate modules for your own resources in admin area
  • Meta information that can be stored on your resources without changing the database tables
  • Easy to add filters to resource lists in the admin
  • Global search feature that you can easily tie your own resources into
  • Global "recycle bin" where admins can un-delete or purge soft-deleted resources
  • Cookie Consent framework to help you comply with GDPR
  • Customizable charts and stats for the dashboard
  • Easy log and system info viewers

docs.title: Filters
docs.text:
Filtering allows you to specify which columns can be filtered and then pass your model to a view cell that handles the display of the filters. This ensures a consistent look and functionality in the UI while providing the least amount of work when creating a UI.

Read more about Filters

docs.title: Recycler
docs.text:
The Recycler provides an area where users can browse objects that have been deleted and either restore or purge them. The models for these resources must have soft deletes enabled. This section covers registering a resource, localizing column names, and changing how a model is listed, restored and purged.

docs.title: Resource Tabs

docs.title: Row and Bulk Actions
docs.text:
An action is something an admin can do to one record from its row's menu, or to every checked record of a list from the selection bar: delete, ban, publish, export. Bonfire runs every action through one endpoint that checks the permission and the CSRF token, asks for confirmation when the action wants it, skips records the action may not touch, and runs large batches in the background when a queue is available.

The Users list (row and bulk delete) and the Logs list (bulk delete) are built this way.

docs.title: Writing An Action
docs.text:
An action is one class that extends Bonfire\Actions\Action:

use Bonfire\Actions\Action;
use Bonfire\Actions\ActionContext;
use Bonfire\Actions\ActionResult;
use Bonfire\Actions\Confirm;
use Bonfire\Actions\Placement;
use Bonfire\Users\User;

class BanUsers extends Action
{
    public string    $label      = 'Ban';
    public string    $icon       = 'fas fa-ban';
    public string    $permission = 'users.manage-admins';
    public Placement $placement  = Placement::Both;
    public bool      $danger     = true;

    public function confirm(): ?Confirm
    {
        return Confirm::make('Ban {count} users?')
            ->body('They are signed out and cannot sign in until unbanned.')
            ->button('Ban');
    }

    public function allows(User $actor, object $record): bool
    {
        return $actor->id !== $record->id;
    }

    public function handle(ActionContext $context): ActionResult
    {
        foreach ($context->entities() as $user) {
            $user->ban();
        }

        return ActionResult::message('{count} users banned.');
    }
}

label and icon (a Font Awesome class) are shown on the action's button.

permission is needed to see and run the action. Leave it empty for anyone who can reach the admin area. Add a new permission to your app's AuthGroups config.

placement is where the action is offered: Placement::Row in each row's menu, Placement::Bulk in the selection bar, or Placement::Both.

danger styles the action as destructive, in red.

confirm() returns what to ask before the action runs, or null to run straight away. {count} in the title becomes the number of records. ->typeToConfirm() makes the admin type that number before a large destructive run.

allows() decides, per record, whether the action may touch it. Records it rejects, and selected records that no longer exist, are skipped and reported ("3 users banned. Skipped 1.") rather than failing the batch.

handle() does the work and returns an ActionResult::message(), or ActionResult::error() when it fails. {count} in the message becomes the number of records handled. A thrown exception is logged, and the admin sees an "Unknown error" message.

The action's name in its URL comes from the class name: BanUsers is ban-users.

Warning

handle() may run in a queue worker, where there is no request, session or signed-in user. Use only what the context gives you: $context->entities() (the records, one at a time), $context->chunks() (the records, a chunk of up to 100 at a time) and $context->actor() (the admin who started the run).

docs.title: Deleting
docs.text:
Bonfire\Actions\DeleteAction is a ready-made delete: a red Delete that asks first and deletes a chunk at a time. Extend it with how your records are deleted, and usually your own permission and wording:

use Bonfire\Actions\DeleteAction;

class DeletePhotos extends DeleteAction
{
    public string $permission = 'photos.delete';

    protected function delete(array $records): void
    {
        model(PhotoModel::class)->delete(array_map(static fn ($photo) => $photo->id, $records));
    }
}

Override confirm() for your own question and deleted() for the message once it's done. See Bonfire\Users\Actions\DeleteUsers for a complete example.

docs.title: Registering Actions
docs.text:
Actions belong to a named list. Register them in your module's initAdmin(), saying where the list's records come from:

use Bonfire\Actions\ModelSource;

public function initAdmin()
{
    service('actions')->for('photos')
        ->records(new ModelSource(PhotoModel::class))
        ->add(new DeletePhotos());
}

ModelSource finds records by primary key through a model. For records that don't live in a model, implement Bonfire\Actions\RecordSource, which has one method, find(array $ids): array; the Logs list's LogStore is an example.

Any module may add actions to any list, including Bonfire's own. These lists exist:

List Records users Bonfire\Users\User logs Objects whose id is a log file's name 
service('actions')->for('users')->add(new BanUsers());

docs.title: Showing Actions In A List
docs.text:
Two view components render a list's actions for the signed-in admin, leaving out those they lack the permission for.

<x-row-actions> renders a row's menu. Pass the list and the record's ID. Anything in its slot, like an Edit link, comes first:

<td class="text-end">
    <x-row-actions list="photos" id="<?= $photo->id ?>">
        <li><a href="<?= url_to('photo-edit', $photo->id) ?>" class="dropdown-item">Edit</a></li>
    </x-row-actions>
</td>

The row menu shows only the actions the admin may run on that record: their permission, and their allows() for it. To ask allows(), the component needs the record. Hand the page's records to the list with showing() before the rows render, or the component loads each one through the list's record source, one lookup per row.

<x-bulk-actions> goes inside <x-selection-bar>, in a form whose row checkboxes are named selects[] with the record's ID as their value. Ask the list's selectable() whether to show them at all: it is true when the admin may run any of its bulk actions. Given a record, it says whether any of those actions allows() it:

<?php
$actionList = service('actions')->for('photos')->showing($photos);
$selectable = $actionList->selectable(auth()->user());
?>
<form method="post">
    <?= csrf_field() ?>
    <table class="table bf-table">
        <!-- ... -->
        <?php if ($selectable) : ?>
            <td class="bf-select-cell">
                <input type="checkbox" name="selects[]" value="<?= $photo->id ?>" class="form-check-input"
                    <?= $actionList->selectable(auth()->user(), $photo) ? '' : 'disabled' ?>>
            </td>
        <?php endif ?>
        <!-- ... -->
    </table>

    <?php if ($selectable) : ?>
        <x-selection-bar>
            <x-bulk-actions list="photos" />
        </x-selection-bar>
    <?php endif ?>
</form>

docs.title: Confirmation
docs.text:
With JavaScript, an action that asks first opens <x-confirm-dialog>, a dialog that is in the Admin layout once. It shows the title with the count filled in, the body, and a red button for dangerous actions.

Without JavaScript, the action's button posts straight to the endpoint, which answers with a confirmation page holding the same question and a button to go ahead. Either way, an action never runs until it's confirmed.

The dialog also handles two other kinds of confirmation, so they look the same:

  • htmx's hx-confirm attribute: <a hx-get="..." hx-confirm="Remove the image?">.
  • A data-confirm attribute on any link or submit button: the link is followed, or the form submitted, once the admin confirms. data-confirm-button sets the button's label and data-confirm-danger="1" makes it red.
<a href="<?= url_to('photo-purge', $photo->id) ?>" data-confirm="Purge this photo?" data-confirm-danger="1">Purge</a>

docs.title: Running In The Background
docs.text:
Each action decides whether its runs are queued with its $queue property:

  • Queue::Auto (the default) runs in the request, unless it has more records than $queueAbove (500 by default).
  • Queue::Always always queues.
  • Queue::Never always runs in the request.
use Bonfire\Actions\Queue;

class ExportPhotos extends Action
{
    public Queue $queue = Queue::Always;
    // ...
}

Queued runs need the codeigniter4/queue package, which Bonfire suggests but doesn't require:

composer require codeigniter4/queue
php spark migrate --all
php spark queue:work bonfire-actions

Bonfire registers its bonfire-action job with the queue for you. Keep a queue:work bonfire-actions worker running, or queued runs will wait forever.

Without the package, Queue::Auto runs in the request, a chunk at a time, and Queue::Always refuses with a message explaining what's missing.

A queued run is recorded in the action_runs table with its totals and status. The admin who started it sees a toast that shows its progress, updated every two seconds, and its message once it ends. service('actionRuns') owns this lifecycle: the endpoint, the queue job and <x-action-run> all go through it.

docs.title: Admin Controllers, Views and Themes
docs.text: This page shows how to render an admin page inside the Admin theme, lay out its view, and change the theme's own files without losing your changes when Bonfire updates.

docs.title: Render an admin page
docs.text:
Extend Bonfire\Core\AdminController and return $this->render() with the full, namespaced name of your view:

namespace App\Modules\Blog\Controllers;

use App\Modules\Blog\Models\PostModel;
use Bonfire\Core\AdminController;

class PostController extends AdminController
{
    public function list()
    {
        return $this->render('App\Modules\Blog\Views\list', [
            'posts' => model(PostModel::class)->findAll(),
        ]);
    }
}

AdminController uses the Bonfire\View\Themeable trait with its $theme property set to Admin. render() points the view renderer at the themes/Admin folder, adds a $viewMeta variable to your data (the layout uses it for the page title and meta tags, see Metadata), and renders the view.

render() takes the same $data and $options arguments as CodeIgniter's view(). A view name with a namespace loads from your module. A name without one, like Search/index, loads from the theme folder.

docs.title: Lay out the view
docs.text:
Start the view by extending the theme's master layout. Because the renderer points at the theme folder, master means themes/Admin/master.php:

<?php $this->extend('master') ?>

<?php $this->section('main') ?>
    <x-page-head title="Posts"></x-page-head>

    <x-admin-box title="All posts">
        <?php foreach ($posts as $post) : ?>
            <p><?= esc($post->title) ?></p>
        <?php endforeach ?>
    </x-admin-box>
<?php $this->endSection() ?>

<?php $this->section('styles') ?>
    <style>.post-draft { opacity: .6; }</style>
<?php $this->endSection() ?>

<?php $this->section('scripts') ?>
    <script>console.log('Posts loaded');</script>
<?php $this->endSection() ?>

The Admin layout renders these sections:

Section Where it goes main The page content, between the header and the footer. styles The end of <head>, after the admin CSS. scripts The end of <body>, after Bootstrap, Alpine.js and htmx have loaded. crumb The page's name in the header breadcrumb. crumbParent The breadcrumb's parent, when the page's URL doesn't sit under a menu item.

Only main is required. See Naming a page in the breadcrumb for crumb and crumbParent, and View Components for the <x-…> tags.

docs.title: Use a different theme
docs.text:
Each folder in themes/ is a theme, named after the folder. To render a controller with another theme, set its $theme property:

use Bonfire\Core\AdminController;

class ReportController extends AdminController
{
    protected $theme = 'Reports';
}

Controllers that extend Bonfire\Core\BaseController use the App theme by default. Any controller can use the Bonfire\View\Themeable trait to get render() and $theme without extending a Bonfire controller.

To pick the theme at runtime, change $this->theme before the first render() call. The trait keeps the renderer it creates on that first call, so later changes have no effect. If the theme folder doesn't exist, render() throws a RuntimeException.

docs.title: Render without a controller
docs.text:
The render() helper does the same work where there is no controller, such as a route closure. Pass the theme name first:

$routes->get('admin/blog/preview', static fn () => render('Admin', 'App\Modules\Blog\Views\preview', [
    'title' => 'Preview',
]));

The theme name must match the folder name exactly, including case. Unlike the trait, the helper doesn't check that the folder exists.

docs.title: Override a theme view
docs.text:
php spark bf:install copies Bonfire's themes into a themes/ folder in your project root, and publishes app/Config/Themes.php pointing at it. Your app renders only this copy, so to change any theme file, edit it in place:

  • themes/Admin/master.php: the page layout
  • themes/Admin/_header.php: the header, breadcrumb and user menu
  • themes/Admin/Components/: the <x-…> view components
  • themes/Admin/Search/: the global search result views
  • themes/Admin/css/ and themes/Admin/js/: the admin styles and scripts

To keep Bonfire's version alongside your own, copy the theme to a new folder, for example themes/MyAdmin, edit the copy, and point your controllers at it with $theme. Bonfire's own admin pages keep using Admin.

docs.title: When Bonfire updates
docs.text:
composer update changes the themes in vendor/lonnieezell/bonfire/themes/, never your copy in themes/. Your edits are safe, but your copy also doesn't get Bonfire's fixes and new features. Why Themes Are Published Into Your App explains this trade-off.

When an update changes a theme in a way your copy needs, the changelog marks it (breaking change) and says what to change, and php spark notify:breaking-changes warns you after composer update (see Updating Bonfire). To find every difference between the two versions, compare the folders:

diff -ru vendor/lonnieezell/bonfire/themes/Admin themes/Admin

docs.title: Creating an Admin Module
docs.text:
The bulk of your work in the admin area will likely be done creating new modules of code. Modules are groups of code centered around a single task or resource, like Users, Photos, etc. For the most part, admin modules are like any other bit of module CodeIgniter code, except for a new Module.php file that helps the module integrate into the admin area. Other than that you will be able to take advantage of solutions that allow your code to integrate directly into settings pages, be part of the global search results, automatically display and manage filtering of a resource list, or show up in the Recycler.

A good module to look at when creating your own is the Bonfire's own Users module (src/Users). You can also look at an example module Pages, which is an implementation of a module of Bonfire 2 admin panel for administration of pages on a website.

docs.title: Configuring Module Locations
docs.text:
In order for Bonfire to discover your modules, you need to specify one or more locations that you plan on storing the modules. No location is set by default: the app/Modules entry in Config\Bonfire ships commented out, so uncomment it (or add your own, see below) before Bonfire will find your modules. As an example, we could create a Blog folder to store our new blog package. You would then need to create the standard directories, Config, Controllers, Models and Views at the very least. A Module.php file is also expected to live here, which we will look at in more detail a little later. The directory structure would look like:

app/
    Modules/
        Blog/
            Config/
            Controllers/
            Models/
            Views/
            Module.php

All files within the Blog directory would be expected to live within the App\Modules\{ModuleName} namespace, i.e. App\Modules\Blog\Config\Routes. To enable discovery, uncomment the entry in the $appModules setting of Config\Bonfire. You can customize the namespace by changing its key.

public $appModules = [
    'App\Modules' => APPPATH .'Modules',
];

For example, if I would prefer the modules to simply live within my company's namespace, Acme, I could edit the key to reflect that:

public $appModules = [
    'Acme' => APPPATH .'Modules',
];

If you have multiple locations you need to keep modules, you can add multiple entries here and they will all be automatically discovered and registered within Bonfire.

Bonfire caches the modules it finds in these locations for a minute. To pick up a new module folder straight away, run php spark cache:clear.

docs.title: Modules in Composer packages
docs.text:
$appModules treats every folder in a location as a module, so it doesn't fit a Composer package that is a single module. List such a module in $packageModules instead. Each entry maps the module's own namespace to the directory that holds its Module.php:

public array $packageModules = [
    'Acme\Blog' => ROOTPATH . 'vendor/acme/blog/src',
];

Composer already autoloads the package's classes, so Bonfire only needs to find its Module.php. An entry whose directory or Module.php is missing is skipped.

A package can register itself, so the app using it changes nothing. Add a Config\Registrar class to the package with a Bonfire() method, and CodeIgniter merges what it returns into Config\Bonfire, including an app's published copy:

namespace Acme\Blog\Config;

class Registrar
{
    public static function Bonfire(): array
    {
        return [
            'packageModules' => ['Acme\Blog' => realpath(__DIR__ . '/..')],
        ];
    }
}

CodeIgniter only finds registrars in Composer packages while Config\Modules::$discoverInComposer is true, its default.

docs.title: The Module File
docs.text:
The Module file handles initialization functions when the admin is loaded. It allows the module to create new menus, insert itself into the existing sidebar menus, etc. The initAdmin method is where all of the setup for displaying and admin page should be done.

Bonfire boots once per web request and calls one of two methods on every module:

  • initAdmin() on a request inside the admin area (ADMIN_AREA). The sidebar menus and dashboard widgets exist only then, so add menu items and widgets here.
  • initFront() on every other routed web request. Use it for setup your module needs on public pages.

Bonfire boots from the bonfire filter, so neither runs where filters don't: 404 pages, pages served from CodeIgniter's page cache, and CLI commands that don't boot Bonfire themselves. How Bonfire Fits Into a Request explains where booting sits among Bonfire's filters.

namespace Acme\Blog;

use Bonfire\Core\BaseModule;
use Bonfire\Menus\MenuItem;

class Module extends BaseModule
{
    public function initAdmin()
    {
        //
    }
}

docs.title: Adding a Menu Item
docs.text:
The main side navigation in the admin consists of three primary menu collections:

  • a main Content collection where you would place the main page for managing a resource (like Users)
  • the Settings collection where your module's settings pages should live.
  • the Tools collection which holds miscellaneous things that are helpful, but not needed on a daily basis.

Menu items are added to the sidebar using the menus service. This example from the core Users module adds the Users page to the content collection:

$item = new MenuItem([
    'title'           => lang('Users.usersModTitle'),
    'namedRoute'      => 'user-list',
    'fontAwesomeIcon' => 'fas fa-users',
    'permission'      => 'users.list',
]);
service('menus')->menu('sidebar')->collection('content')->addItem($item);

namedRoute must be a named route defined in your module's Config/Routes.php. Users without permission don't see the item. See Menus for every key, collections, custom menus and reordering with $menuWeights.

Every menu item the user may see also shows up in the ⌘K / Ctrl+K command palette, and the header's breadcrumb names the active item (and its collection, when that collection is collapsible).

docs.title: Naming a page in the breadcrumb
docs.text:
A page below a menu item, like a single record's edit form, can add itself to the breadcrumb with a crumb view section. The breadcrumb then reads "active menu item › crumb". When the page's URL doesn't sit under any menu item, name the parent too with crumbParent:

<?php $this->extend('master') ?>

<?php $this->section('crumbParent') ?><?= lang('Tools.logsModTitle') ?><?php $this->endSection() ?>
<?php $this->section('crumb') ?><?= esc($logFilePretty) ?><?php $this->endSection() ?>

docs.title: Controllers and views
docs.text: Your module's pages are ordinary CodeIgniter controllers and views, rendered inside the Admin theme. See Admin Controllers, Views and Themes for AdminController, the master layout and its sections, and changing the theme's own files.

docs.title: Dashboard Widgets
docs.text:
Anything an admin can place on the dashboard is a widget. A module adds widgets from its initAdmin() in one of two ways:

  • Write a widget: implement Bonfire\Dashboard\DashboardWidget. You choose its title, icon, sizes, settings and markup. Bonfire's own widgets, such as Quick Links (Bonfire\Dashboard\Widgets\QuickLinksWidget), are built this way.
  • Add a stat card or chart: describe a number or a chart with a StatsItem or ChartsItem, and Bonfire draws it.

Any widget a module adds is not on the default layout: admins add it from the widget library, or a site admin puts it on the site default. To ship it on the default layout, add its id to the $layout of your Config\Dashboard.

docs.title: Writing a widget
docs.text:
use Bonfire\Dashboard\DashboardWidget;
use Bonfire\Dashboard\Size;
use Bonfire\Dashboard\SizeRange;
use Bonfire\Dashboard\WidgetField;
use Bonfire\Dashboard\WidgetValues;

class OpenOrders implements DashboardWidget
{
    public function id(): string { return 'shop:openOrders'; }
    public function title(): string { return 'Open orders'; }
    public function icon(): string { return 'fas fa-cart-shopping'; }
    public function group(): string { return 'Shop'; }
    public function description(): string { return 'Orders waiting to ship'; }
    public function sizes(): SizeRange { return new SizeRange(Size::Half, Size::Quarter, Size::TwoThirds); }
    public function permission(): ?string { return 'shop.orders'; }

    public function fields(): array
    {
        return [
            WidgetField::number('limit', 'Orders to show', default: 5, min: 1, max: 20),
            WidgetField::toggle('showTotals', 'Show totals', default: true),
        ];
    }

    public function render(WidgetValues $values): string
    {
        return view('Shop\Views\open_orders', [
            'orders'     => model(OrderModel::class)->open($values->get('limit')),
            'showTotals' => $values->get('showTotals'),
        ]);
    }
}
  • id is stored in admins' saved layouts, so keep it unique and never change it. Prefix it with your module's name.
  • group is the library heading it is listed under: your module's name. The library lists modules in name order. The type keys quickLinks, stats, charts and custom still work, each under its own heading.
  • sizes is the width it starts at, then the smallest and largest an admin may pick, from Size::Quarter, Third, Half, TwoThirds and Full.
  • permission hides the widget from admins who lack it, in the library and on the dashboard, and drops it from layouts they save. null shows it to every admin.
  • fields are the settings admins may change for the widget on their own dashboard. Return [] when it has none, and its edit-mode tools offer no settings.
  • render is called only when the widget is on the viewer's dashboard, so it may run queries. It gets the value of each field as the viewer placed it.

docs.title: Registering it
docs.text:
public function initAdmin()
{
    service('dashboard')->register(new OpenOrders());
}

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Each WidgetField is one setting, drawn in the widget's settings panel. Bonfire draws the form, checks what is posted, stores each admin's values with their layout, and hands render() the result. Read a value with $values->get('name'), not with setting().

Field Input Value WidgetField::toggle($name, $label, default: …) A switch bool WidgetField::number($name, $label, default: …, min: …, max: …, step: …) A number box int, or float when step is a fraction; kept within min and max WidgetField::choice($name, $label, $options, default: …) Segmented buttons, or a select for more than four options One of the keys of $options (value => label) WidgetField::text($name, $label, default: …) A text box string, trimmed, at most 255 characters

Every field also takes an optional description: shown under its label. A placed widget uses each field's default until an admin changes it. Only values that differ from the default are stored, so changing the default in code later reaches every admin who left the field alone. A value that is not of the field's type, a choice the field does not offer, or the name of a field the widget no longer declares is dropped when the layout is saved, and ignored when it is rendered.

docs.title: Stat cards and charts
docs.text:
For a single number or a chart of one table, add an item to service('widgets') instead of writing a class. Each item becomes a widget with the id stats: or charts: plus its own id.

Give an item its value with addValue(), addValueByFreeQuery() or addDataset(). They store the query and run it only when the dashboard shows the widget, to a viewer who holds its permission. A value passed to the constructor is built every time your module boots, on every admin page.

docs.title: Stat cards
docs.text:
use Bonfire\Widgets\Types\Stats\StatsItem;

public function initAdmin()
{
    $item = new StatsItem([
        'id'         => 'openOrders',
        'title'      => 'Open orders',
        'url'        => ADMIN_AREA . '/orders',
        'faIcon'     => 'fas fa-cart-shopping',
        'permission' => 'shop.orders',
        'module'     => 'Shop',
    ]);
    $item->addValue('orders', "status = 'open'");

    service('widgets')->widget('stats')->collection('stats')->addItem($item);
}
Key Meaning id Unique across the install, and stored in saved layouts: the widget's id is stats: plus this. Never change it. title Shown at the top of the card. url The page the card's "View Detail" link opens. faIcon FontAwesome classes for the icon next to the title. permission Hides the card from admins who lack it, like a widget's permission(). module The library heading it is listed under. Without it, it is listed under Stats. value A value built now, on every admin page. The card prints it unescaped, so it may be HTML. Prefer the methods below. bgColor Accepted, but no longer changes the card.

A stat card is ¼ wide and has one setting, showing the "View Detail" link.

addValue(string $tableName, ?string $whereString = null, string $selectMode = 'count') counts the rows of $tableName whose deleted_at is null, so the table needs a deleted_at column. $whereString adds a condition. $selectMode avg, max, min or sum takes that of the table's value column in place of counting.

addValueByFreeQuery(string $query) runs $query and shows the first column of its first row.

docs.title: Charts
docs.text:
use Bonfire\Widgets\Types\Charts\ChartsItem;

$item = new ChartsItem([
    'id'         => 'ordersByStatus',
    'title'      => 'Orders by status',
    'type'       => 'doughnut',
    'cssClass'   => 'col-6',
    'permission' => 'shop.orders',
    'module'     => 'Shop',
]);
$item->addDataset('orders', 'status', 'id');

service('widgets')->widget('charts')->collection('charts')->addItem($item);
Key Meaning id, title, permission, module As for a stat card, with charts: in place of stats:. Listed under Charts without module. type line, bar, doughnut, pie or polarArea. cssClass Its default width: col-3, col-4, col-6, col-8 or col-12. Anything else starts at half width.

addDataset(string $tableName, string $groupField, string $countField, string $selectMode = 'count') groups the rows of $tableName by $groupField, one label each, and counts $countField in each group. $selectMode avg, max, min or sum takes that of $countField in place of counting. A chart has one dataset.

Each chart has the settings listed in Widget settings.

docs.title: Legacy: view cells
docs.text:
Before widgets, the dashboard showed the view cells listed in the $cells property of the Dashboard config file. That still works, but a cell gets no title, icon, sizes, settings or permission of its own: write a widget instead.

public array $cells = [
    'Bonfire\Widgets\Cells\WidgetCells::stats',
    'Bonfire\Widgets\Cells\WidgetCells::logs',
    'Bonfire\Widgets\Cells\WidgetCells::charts',
];

A cell is a class method that returns HTML:

class ShopCells
{
    public function openOrders()
    {
        return view('Shop\Views\open_orders', [
            'orders' => model(OrderModel::class)->open(),
        ]);
    }
}

Add 'Shop\Cells\ShopCells::openOrders' to $cells and it becomes a full-width widget with the id cell:Shop\Cells\ShopCells::openOrders, listed under Custom, with no permission. The stats, logs and charts cells listed by default don't become widgets: they stand for the stat cards and charts above. When the config's $layout is null, the default layout is the cells of $cells, in order.

docs.title: Moving to a widget
docs.text: To replace a stat card, chart or cell with a widget of your own, give the new widget the id the old one had (for example stats:openOrders or cell:Shop\Cells\ShopCells::openOrders), so saved layouts keep it in place, and stop adding the old item. Quick Links did the same: it keeps the id cell:Bonfire\Dashboard\DashboardCells::quickLinks, so installs whose $cells still lists that cell show it once, where it was.

docs.title: Filters
docs.text: Every collection of items needs to be filtered at some point. Unless you're building a photo gallery or an ecommerce site this might be when presenting posts, users, pages, etc in the admin area. Filtering allows you to specify which columns can be filtered and then pass your model to a view cell that takes care of handling the display of the filters for you. This ensures a consistent look and functionality in the UI while providing the least amount of work when you need to create a UI in a hurry.

docs.title: Specifying Filterable Columns
docs.text:
You specify the available filters within your Model, using a class property named filters.

protected $filters = [
    'column_name' => [
        'title' => 'Column Title',
        'type' => 'radio',
        'options' => ['one' => 'Option 1', 'two' => 'Option 2']
    ],
    'column_two' => [
        'title' => 'Column Title',
        'options' => 'methodName'
    ]
];

The key of each array element is the name of the column that you wish to filter on. The column must be within the table for the model (see below for other options). It is then described by an array with the keys title, options, and optional key type. Title is the display title for that group of options. The options value is typically an array of keys and their display values that the column should be filtered by. The keys must match valid values within the database. Key type signifies if the filter should be composed of checkboxes (default) or radio's. If it is omitted, the default value checkbox would be assumed. In case type => radio is specified, the last option in the options array will be pre-selected in the filter UI, so it should probably contain value representing all entries.

Sometimes you need to pull values from a config file, or another table, etc, in order to provide the list of options. In this case, you can use the string methodName where methodName is a method within the model to call that returns the list of options.

docs.title: Implementing the Filters
docs.text:
If all the columns match directly to columns within the model's database table, then you can make use of the Filterable trait, which implements a basic filter() method for you.

Since model's can get crowded with test data, filter data, custom methods, events, and more, you can split out the filter functionality into a new class that extends the model, placing your custom filter logic within that class.

use App\UserModel;
use Bonfire\Core\Traits\Filterable;

class UserFilter extends UserModel
{
    use Filterable;

    public $filters = [
        ...
    ];

    /**
     * A computed options function
     */
    protected function computeFilterA()
    {
        //
    }
}

docs.title: Complex Filter Columns
docs.text:
There are many times that you'll need to show options that don't directly relate to the model at hand. In this case you must override the filter() method on the model. Within that method you must handle all of the cases for the options you provided manually, returning the query object.

public function filter(array $params)
{
    $query = $this->builder();

    if (isset($params['foo']) && ! empty($params['foo'])) {
        $query->whereIn('foo', $params['foo']);
    }

    return $query;
}

docs.title: Displaying Filters in the Admin
docs.text: There are 4 parts that are needed to get a working, filterable list of resources in the admin area.

docs.title: The Route
docs.text:
The main route for your resource list page must support both GET and POST methods.

$routes->match(['GET', 'POST'], 'users', 'UserController::list', ['as' => 'user-list']);

The controller should then choose between sending either a full HTML page for a regular GET request, or just sending back the table for ajax requests issued via HTMX. You might do it something like:

public function list()
{
    $userModel = model('UserFilter');

    // Performs the actual filtering of the results.
    $userModel->filter($this->request->getPost('filters'));

    $view = $this->request->hasHeader('HX-Request')
        ? $this->viewPrefix .'_table'
        : $this->viewPrefix .'list';

    return $this->render($view, [
        'headers' => [
            'email' => 'Email',
            'name' => 'Name',
            'groups' => 'Groups',
            'last_login' => 'Last Login'
        ],
        'showSelectAll' => true,
        'users' => $userModel->paginate(setting('Site.perPage')),
        'pager' => $userModel->pager,
    ]);
}

docs.title: The View
docs.text:
Within your view there are 3 things to do.

First, ensure that the table with your resource list is wrapped in a div that uses some Alpine.js to attach a filtered status of false to the div. This creates a variable that determines whether the filters list is shown or not.

Second, insert the x-filter-link component into the top of that div. This provides the link that will show/hide the list of filters. This component toggles the filtered value above between true and false.

Finally, call the renderList view cell which inserts the HTML for the list of options, all wrapped in a form that calls your controller method via AJAX and updates the list of items without a page refresh, using some htmx magic. When calling this, you must supply the ID of the div that surrounds the table of results as the target.

Here's how this is used for the list of users within Bonfire.

<div x-data="{filtered: false}">
    <x-filter-link />

    <div class="row">
        <!-- List Users -->
        <div class="col order-2 order-md-1" id="content-list">
            <?= $this->include('Bonfire\Users\Views\_table') ?>
        </div>

        <!-- Filters -->
        <div class="col-auto order-1 order-md-2" x-show="filtered" x-transition.duration.240ms>
            <?= view_cell('Bonfire\Core\Cells\Filters::renderList', 'model=UserFilter target=#content-list') ?>
        </div>
    </div>
</div>

Note that the id of the eleent that contains the included table should be with id="content-list" as it this id is the default target for content replacements by the pager and the filter.

For the admin design's list footer ("Showing X of Y · Previous / Next", loaded through htmx), render the pager with the bonfire_list_hx template inside the replaced element: <?= $pager->links('default', 'bonfire_list_hx') ?>. It takes its hx-target from an ancestor, so put hx-target="#content-list" on an element that wraps the list.

docs.title: Localization
docs.text: Bonfire's admin text comes from language files, so you can change its wording, run it in another language, and translate your own modules the same way. This page shows how. It builds on CodeIgniter's Localization guide.

docs.title: How Bonfire finds a string
docs.text:
Views and controllers call lang('File.key'). lang('Users.usersModTitle') reads the usersModTitle key from a file named Users.php in a Language/{locale}/ folder.

Bonfire keeps those files beside the code that uses them:

File Where it lives in the package Holds Bonfire.php src/Language/{locale}/ Shared admin text: save and delete messages, collection titles. Actions.php, Consent.php, Email.php, Groups.php, Recycler.php, Tools.php, Users.php, Widgets.php src/{Module}/Language/{locale}/ Each module's own text. Auth.php Shield, vendor/codeigniter4/shield/src/Language/{locale}/ Login, registration and magic link text.

Bonfire registers every module folder as a namespace, so CodeIgniter searches each module's Language/ folder too. When more than one namespace has the same file, CodeIgniter merges them key by key, and files under app/ are merged last. A key in your app/ file wins; every key you leave out still comes from Bonfire.

When a key has no translation for the current locale, CodeIgniter tries the next locale in this order, and shows the first one it finds:

  1. The full locale, like fr-CA.
  2. The language without the region, fr.
  3. English, en.
  4. The key itself, like Users.usersModTitle.

docs.title: Override a string
docs.text:
To change Bonfire's wording, create a file of the same name under app/Language/{locale}/ and put in only the keys you're changing.

To call users "members", create app/Language/en/Users.php:

<?php

return [
    'usersModTitle' => 'Members',
    'userGenitive'  => 'member',
];

Reload the admin. The Users menu item now says Members, and messages like "Unable to find the member." use the new word. All the other Users.* keys still come from Bonfire, so new keys added in a Bonfire update show up without you having to touch this file.

The same works for any file in the table above, including Shield's Auth.php. Look up the key names in the package's en file.

Note

Some strings take placeholders, like 'resourceSaved' => 'The {0} has been saved.'. Keep the placeholders in your version. lang() fills them in, in order.

docs.title: Add a locale
docs.text:
Bonfire ships translations in Spanish, Italian, Lithuanian and Russian alongside English. To run the admin in another language, French for example:

  1. Copy Bonfire's English files into a folder named after the locale:

    mkdir -p app/Language/fr
cp vendor/lonnieezell/bonfire/src/Language/en/*.php \
   vendor/lonnieezell/bonfire/src/*/Language/en/*.php \
   app/Language/fr/

    Only copy whole files for a locale Bonfire doesn't ship. For es, it, lt or ru, a copied English file would replace the translations Bonfire already has; add only the missing keys instead, as in Override a string.

  2. Translate the values in each copied file. Leave the keys as they are.

  3. Tell CodeIgniter about the locale in app/Config/App.php:

    public string $defaultLocale = 'fr';

public array $supportedLocales = ['fr', 'en'];

    To pick the locale from each visitor's browser instead, set $negotiateLocale = true;. CodeIgniter then chooses from $supportedLocales.

Shield already ships Auth.php in many languages, French included, so you don't need to copy it. For CodeIgniter's own strings, like the pager's, install the community translations:

composer require codeigniter4/translations

You don't have to translate every key at once. Any key missing from your files falls back to English, so a partial translation still works.

docs.title: Translate your own module
docs.text:
Give your module its own language file, named after the module, in a Language/{locale}/ folder inside the module. For a Blog module in app/Modules/Blog:

app/Modules/Blog/
├── Language/
│   ├── en/
│   │   └── Blog.php
│   └── fr/
│       └── Blog.php
├── Module.php
└── ...

app/Modules/Blog/Language/en/Blog.php:

<?php

return [
    'title'      => 'Blog',
    'posts'      => 'Posts',
    'postSaved'  => 'The post "{0}" has been saved.',
    'postCount'  => '{0, plural, =0 {No posts} one {# post} other {# posts}}',
];

Bonfire finds the folder once your module is loaded through Config\Bonfire::$appModules (see Creating an Admin Module). Use the strings anywhere in the module, including menu items:

service('menus')->menu('sidebar')->collection('content')->addItem(new MenuItem([
    'title'      => lang('Blog.posts'),
    'namedRoute' => 'blog-posts',
]));

return redirect()->back()->with('message', lang('Blog.postSaved', [$post->title]));

<?= lang('Blog.postCount', [$total]) ?>

{0} placeholders and ICU plural rules need PHP's intl extension. Without it, lang() returns the string with the placeholders still in it.

Warning

Don't name your file after one of Bonfire's: Bonfire, Actions, Auth, Consent, Email, Groups, Recycler, Tools, Users or Widgets. CodeIgniter would merge your keys into Bonfire's, and a matching key in your module would change Bonfire's text.

docs.title: Check your translations
docs.text:
Set $defaultLocale to the locale and open the admin pages you translated. A string that shows in English has no translation for that locale. A string that shows as File.key has no English line either, which usually means a typo in the key or the file name.

The admin theme prints the current locale in <html lang="…">, which you can check in the page source.

docs.title: Contribute a translation to Bonfire
docs.text:
Translations of Bonfire itself are welcome, including partial ones. Put each file beside its English version in the package: src/Language/{locale}/Bonfire.php and src/{Module}/Language/{locale}/{Module}.php. Open a pull request on GitHub.

The shipped translations have gaps. Spanish has only Bonfire.php, Actions.php exists only in English, and the other files lack many of the newer English keys. Those show in English until someone translates them.

docs.title: Menus
docs.text: The admin sidebar is a menu. Your module adds pages to it from its Module::initAdmin(), and it can build menus of its own. This page lists every menu class, key and method. For where initAdmin() sits in a module, see Creating an Admin Module.

docs.title: How menus fit together
docs.text:
Class What it is Get one with Bonfire\Menus\Manager Holds every menu by name. service('menus') Bonfire\Menus\Menu A named menu, like sidebar. Holds collections. service('menus')->menu('sidebar') Bonfire\Menus\MenuCollection A group of items, like the sidebar's Settings. ->collection('settings') Bonfire\Menus\MenuItem One link. new MenuItem([...])

Menus only exist on admin requests. Bonfire creates the built-in ones before it calls initAdmin(), so add items there and nowhere else.

docs.title: Built-in menus
docs.text:
Bonfire creates two menus:

  • sidebar, the admin's side navigation, with three collections:

    Collection Title Shown as content Content One sidebar link per item, with its icon. Also lists the items in the Quick Links dashboard widget. settings Settings One sidebar link (fas fa-cog) to the first item the user may see. The settings pages list the rest with <x-settings-layout>. tools Tools A collapsible group (fas fa-toolbox) of item titles.

  • iconbar, which is empty. The Admin theme doesn't render it.

Every item the user may see in a sidebar collection also appears in the ⌘K / Ctrl+K command palette.

docs.title: Keys
docs.text:
Pass the keys as an array to the constructor. Each key calls the setter of the same name, in array order.

Key Type Default Setter Effect title string none setTitle() Text of the link. Required. The sidebar prints it without escaping, so escape text that comes from users. namedRoute string none setNamedRoute() Sets the URL with route_to(). Required unless you pass url. It's also the key $menuWeights looks up. url string none setUrl() Sets the URL directly. A URL without :// gets a leading /. When you pass both url and namedRoute, the later one in the array wins. fontAwesomeIcon string none setFontAwesomeIcon() FontAwesome classes, like fas fa-users. iconUrl string none setIconUrl() URL of an image icon. Used only when there's no fontAwesomeIcon. Currently broken, see Limitations. altText string none setAltText() Stored, but the Admin theme doesn't use it. See Limitations. weight int 0 setWeight() Sort order inside the collection. Larger weights appear later; equal weights sort by title. $menuWeights overrides it, see Ordering. permission string none setPermission() A permission the user needs to see the item. Leave it out to show the item to everyone. 
use Bonfire\Menus\MenuItem;

$item = new MenuItem([
    'title'           => lang('Blog.posts'),
    'namedRoute'      => 'blog-posts',
    'fontAwesomeIcon' => 'fas fa-newspaper',
    'permission'      => 'blog.list',
    'weight'          => 10,
]);

service('menus')->menu('sidebar')->collection('content')->addItem($item);

Every setter returns the item, so you can build one fluently instead:

$item = (new MenuItem())
    ->setTitle('Blog Settings')
    ->setUrl(ADMIN_AREA . '/settings/blog')
    ->setFontAwesomeIcon('fas fa-newspaper')
    ->setPermission('blog.settings');

An item built this way isn't matched by $menuWeights, because only the namedRoute key in the constructor registers the route for it.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
Method Returns title() The title. url() The URL. altText() The alt text. weight() The weight, 0 when unset. userCanSee() true when the item has no permission or the logged-in user has it. icon(string $class = '') The icon tag: <i class="…"> for FontAwesome, <img> for iconUrl, or ''. $class adds classes to it.

You can also read each of these methods as a property: $item->title, $item->url, $item->icon.

docs.title: MenuCollection
docs.text: A MenuCollection is a MenuItem with a name and a list of items. It accepts the same keys and setters, so it can have a title and an icon. A collection has no URL.

docs.title: Creating collections
docs.text:
Create collections on a Menu:

Method Does createCollection(string $name, string $title) Adds a new, empty collection and returns it. Doesn't check whether $name exists. collect(string $name, array $items) Adds $items to the collection called $name, creating it first (titled ucfirst($name)) if needed. Returns the collection. collection(string $name) The collection called $name, or null. collections() Every collection, in the order they were created.

The sidebar shows collections in the order they were created, so a new one appears after Tools. This adds a collapsible Blog group to the sidebar:

$sidebar = service('menus')->menu('sidebar');

$sidebar->createCollection('blog', lang('Blog.title'))
    ->setFontAwesomeIcon('fas fa-newspaper')
    ->setCollapsible();

$sidebar->collect('blog', [
    new MenuItem(['title' => lang('Blog.posts'), 'namedRoute' => 'blog-posts', 'permission' => 'blog.list']),
    new MenuItem(['title' => lang('Blog.categories'), 'namedRoute' => 'blog-categories', 'permission' => 'blog.list']),
]);

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Method Default Effect setName(string $name) '' The name collection() finds it by. isActive() uses it too. setCollapsible(bool $collapse = true) false Show the collection as a group that opens to list its item titles. setPageNav(bool $pageNav = true) false Show one sidebar link to the first item the user may see instead of the items. Your pages then need their own nav. <x-settings-layout> provides it for settings only. Takes priority over setCollapsible().

Read them back with name(), isCollapsible() and hasPageNav().

docs.title: Items
docs.text:
Method Does addItem(MenuItem $item) Adds one item. addItems(array $items) Adds several items. removeItem(string $title) Removes the first item with that title. removeAllItems() Empties the collection. items() The items, sorted by weight, then title. Includes items the user can't see. hasVisibleItems() true when the user may see at least one item. The sidebar skips collections without one. firstVisibleItem() The first item, by weight, the user may see, or null. isActive() true when the current URL starts with ADMIN_AREA/{name}.

To take a built-in page out of the sidebar, remove it by its title:

service('menus')->menu('sidebar')->collection('tools')->removeItem(lang('Tools.logsModTitle'));

docs.title: Menu
docs.text:
Method Does addItem(MenuItem $item) Adds an item outside any collection. Nothing renders these, see Limitations. items() Every top-level item and collection, in the order added. activeItem() The visible item whose URL is the longest match for the start of the current URL, or null. activeTrail() The titles for the breadcrumb: the collection's title (for collapsible collections) and the active item's title. Empty when nothing matches.

The collection methods are listed under Creating collections.

docs.title: Custom menus
Ordering with $menuWeights
docs.text:
$menuWeights in app/Config/Bonfire.php sets weights by named route, so you can reorder items without editing the modules that add them:

public $menuWeights = [
    'user-list'   => 1,
    'blog-posts'  => 2,
    'recycler'    => 1,
    'sys-info'    => 2,
];
  • A listed route's weight replaces the item's weight.
  • An item matches only when the namedRoute key was passed to its constructor.
  • Weights only sort items within their collection. They can't reorder collections, so Content, Settings and Tools stay where they are.
  • Bonfire reads the value with setting('Bonfire.menuWeights'), so a value saved through the settings library replaces the config.

The Configuration Reference lists the key with Bonfire's other settings.

docs.title: The Admin theme
docs.text: The rendering described on this page is the stock Admin theme's: Components/sidebar.php, _palette.php and _header.php. Your install has its own copy of the theme, which you may have changed. See Why Themes Are Published Into Your App.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• iconUrl icons don't appear. The tag uses href instead of src (#727).
  • altText isn't rendered anywhere (#728).
  • Items added with Menu::addItem() don't appear in the sidebar, the palette or the breadcrumb. Put every item in a collection (#729).
  • Collapsible groups list item titles only, without icons.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
Bonfire uses Shield groups and permissions. A permission, like users.edit, names one thing a user may do. A group, like admin, works like a role. The permission matrix says which permissions each group grants. Your module checks a permission with auth()->user()->can('forum.moderate'), and only users in a group that grants it, or users given it directly, get through.

Every install publishes its own app/Config/AuthGroups.php, so a module should not ask developers to edit that file. Instead, it declares its permissions, and the groups they go to by default, from its own Config\Registrar.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text:
$groups in app/Config/AuthGroups.php defines five groups:

Group Title For superadmin Super Admin Complete control of the site. admin Admin Day to day administrators of the site. developer Developer Site programmers. user User General users of the site. Often customers. beta Beta User Has access to beta-level features.

New users join $defaultGroup, which is user. The user group grants no permissions, so it can't enter the admin area.

docs.title: Permissions and the default matrix
docs.text:
$permissions lists every permission Bonfire uses, and $matrix grants them to groups. Shield refuses to give a user a permission that isn't in $permissions, and the admin screens only list those. The table shows the default matrix. The user group is left out because it has none.

Permission Lets a user superadmin admin developer beta admin.access Enter the admin area. Login also sends these users to the admin. ✓ ✓ ✓ admin.settings Open the General, Email and System Info settings ✓ ✓ groups.settings List groups and edit their details ✓ ✓ ✓ groups.edit Change a group's permissions ✓ users.list See the Users menu item, list users and see the user dashboard widgets ✓ ✓ ✓ users.view Open a user's Permissions tab ✓ users.create Create users ✓ ✓ ✓ users.edit Edit users, their groups and permissions, and ban them ✓ ✓ ✓ users.delete Delete users ✓ ✓ users.manage-admins Manage admins (see Managing groups in the admin) ✓ users.settings Open the Users settings ✓ ✓ ✓ beta.access Nothing in Bonfire checks it. Use it for your own beta features. ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ site.viewOffline Browse the site while it's offline ✓ ✓ widgets.settings Save and reset the site's default dashboard ✓ ✓ ✓ consent.settings Open the Consent settings ✓ ✓ ✓ recycler.view Open the Recycler ✓ ✓ logs.view Read the logs and see the log widgets ✓ ✓ ✓ logs.manage Delete logs ✓ ✓ me.edit Edit their own profile ✓ ✓ ✓ me.security Change their own password ✓ ✓ ✓

The matrix grants superadmin wildcards such as users.*, so it also gets any new permission that starts with one of those prefixes.

docs.title: Checking a permission
docs.text:
can() returns true when any of the user's groups grants the permission, or the user was given it directly. Pass more than one permission to check whether the user has any of them.

In a controller, check before doing the work. Bonfire's own controllers send the user back with an error:

public function index()
{
    if (! auth()->user()->can('forum.access')) {
        return redirect()->to(ADMIN_AREA)->with('error', lang('Bonfire.notAuthorized'));
    }

    // ...
}

In a view, hide the controls a user can't use:

<?php if (auth()->user()->can('forum.moderate')) : ?>
    <a href="<?= site_url(ADMIN_AREA . '/forum/hidden') ?>" class="btn btn-outline-secondary">Hidden posts</a>
<?php endif ?>

To show a menu item only to users with a permission, give it a permission key. See Creating an admin module.

$item = new MenuItem([
    'title'           => 'Forum',
    'namedRoute'      => 'forum-list',
    'fontAwesomeIcon' => 'fas fa-comments',
    'permission'      => 'forum.access',
]);

A menu permission only hides the link

Anyone who can enter the admin area can still type the page's URL. Check the permission in the controller too.

Every route under the admin area also needs admin.access. Bonfire's admin filter checks it before your controller runs and sends other users to the home page. How Bonfire Fits Into a Request shows where it runs among Bonfire's other filters.

docs.title: Declaring permissions
docs.text:
Add a Config/Registrar.php to your module with an AuthGroups() method. CodeIgniter merges the permissions it returns into Config\AuthGroups, including the install's published copy, on every request:

namespace Acme\Forum\Config;

class Registrar
{
    public static function AuthGroups(): array
    {
        return [
            'permissions' => [
                'forum.access'   => 'Can view the forum admin',
                'forum.moderate' => 'Can hide and delete posts',
            ],
        ];
    }
}

Settings → Groups lists them with the rest, grouped by the part before the dot.

Prefix every permission with your module's name

When two lists have the same key, the registrar's value wins. A permission named admin.access would replace the install's own. Name yours forum.*, shop.* and so on.

CodeIgniter only looks for Config/Registrar.php at the root of a namespace it knows about. A module in a Composer package is found as long as Config\Modules::$discoverInComposer is true, its default. A module in app/Modules/Forum is not, because its namespace root is app/. Add the module's namespace to app/Config/Autoload.php so CodeIgniter finds its registrar:

public $psr4 = [
    APP_NAMESPACE      => APPPATH,
    'App\Modules\Forum' => APPPATH . 'Modules/Forum',
];

docs.title: Default grants
docs.text:
A module can also say which groups should get its permissions. Return them as moduleGrants, keyed by your module's name and then by group:

public static function AuthGroups(): array
{
    return [
        'permissions' => [
            // ...
        ],
        'moduleGrants' => [
            'forum' => [
                'superadmin' => ['forum.*'],
                'admin'      => ['forum.access', 'forum.moderate'],
            ],
        ],
    ];
}

Grants are not added to the groups on every request. Once a group is saved in Settings → Groups, Shield keeps the whole permission matrix in the database, and it would ignore them anyway. Instead, the grants are applied by:

php spark bonfire:permissions

The command adds each grant once and remembers it. If an admin later takes a permission away from a group, running the command again does not give it back. A grant for a group the install doesn't have is skipped, and the command says so.

When the command adds a grant, it saves the whole matrix to the database, just as saving a group does. From then on, changes to $matrix in app/Config/AuthGroups.php are ignored.

bf:install runs the command for you. After you add a module or update one that declares new grants, run it yourself.

docs.title: Managing groups in the admin
docs.text:
Settings → Groups lists every group with its alias, how many users are in it and how many permissions it grants. It needs groups.settings. Click a group to edit its title and description.

The group's Permissions tab has a switch for each permission, grouped by prefix. It needs groups.edit. Saving it stores the whole matrix in the database, so from then on changes to $matrix in app/Config/AuthGroups.php are ignored.

To give a single user extra permissions, open the user and use their Permissions tab. The user keeps everything their groups grant as well.

users.manage-admins guards the admins themselves. A user without it can still edit users, but can't:

  • add a user to the admin or superadmin group, or take one out
  • give a user a users.* permission they don't already have
  • ban an admin, or delete a user who has users.manage-admins

docs.title: Adding a group
docs.text:
The admin has no screen for adding a group. Add it to $groups in app/Config/AuthGroups.php, and add the permissions it should start with to $matrix:

public array $groups = [
    // ...
    'editor' => [
        'title'       => 'Editor',
        'description' => 'Writes and publishes content.',
    ],
];

public array $matrix = [
    // ...
    'editor' => [
        'admin.access',
        'me.*',
    ],
];

Saving a group's details in Settings → Groups stores the whole list of groups in the database, just as saving its permissions stores the matrix. After that, Bonfire reads the groups from the database and ignores $groups. On an install where that has happened, add the group with setting() instead, for example from a migration:

$groups = setting('AuthGroups.groups');

$groups['editor'] = [
    'title'       => 'Editor',
    'description' => 'Writes and publishes content.',
];

setting('AuthGroups.groups', $groups);

Then grant its permissions on the group's Permissions tab.

docs.title: The Recycler
docs.text:
The Recycler provides an area where users can browse objects that have been deleted and either restore or purge them. The models for these resources must have soft deletes enabled. By default, only users are displayed here. 

// In the model:
protected $useSoftDeletes = true;

docs.title: Registering A Resource
docs.text:
The Recycler must be told which models it should display. You do not need to do anything special with a model before registering. A module registers its resources in the initAdmin() method of its Module.php: 

public function initAdmin()
{
    service('recycler')->register('photos', 'Photos', PhotoModel::class, [
        'title', 'caption',
    ]);
}

The arguments are, in order:

alias is what you would use to specify the default resource to show when visiting the Recycler, and is part of the URLs for restoring and purging.

label is the name as it should be displayed to the users.

model is the fully qualified classname of the model to get this resource's data from.

columns is an array of database column names for this resource that will be displayed on the Recycler table. This information should only be what is needed to allow someone to find the correct record.

An app can also add a resource, or replace how a module's resource is displayed, within app/Config/Recycler.php. An entry here wins over a module's registration with the same alias:

public $resources = [
    'users' => [
        'label' => 'Users',
        'model' => App\Models\UserModel::class,
        'columns' => [
            'username', 'first_name', 'last_name', 'email'
        ]
    ],
];

docs.title: Localization of Column names in Recycler
docs.text:
To localize the column names, an array recycler should be created in the module's language file, named after the $resource['label'] value (with the .php extension (in case of label 'Users' – Users.php). The array should have sub-keys label and columns, with each column name corresponding $resource['columns'] array value. Example for module Users:

    'recycler' => [
        'label'     => 'Users',
        'columns'   => [
            'id'           => 'ID',
            'username'     => 'User Name',
            'first_name'   => 'Name',
            'last_name'    => 'Surname',
            'email'        => 'Email',
        ],
    ],

If Recycler finds the localized strings, it will use them. Otherwise the original DB column names (capitalized, undescore replaced with space) will be used.

docs.title: Changing How A Model Is Recycled
docs.text:
The Recycler does three things with a resource: it lists the deleted records, restores one, and purges one. By default it lists the records through the model's soft delete field, ordered by the date they were deleted and returned as arrays; restores by setting that field to null; and purges by deleting the record through the model. It uses the primary key and soft delete field of the model, whatever they are called. It will only restore or purge a record that is in the Recycler.

To change any of the three, have the model implement the matching interface from Bonfire\Recycler\Interfaces. Implement only the ones you need. A method with the right name on a model that does not implement the interface is not called.

docs.title: Modifying the Recycler Query
docs.text:
While the basics mentioned above cannot be changed without breaking functionality, you can add requirements, or specify the fields to select, etc. Implement CustomRecyclerQuery and its setupRecycler() method. It doesn't take any arguments, and should return the modified model.

Here is an example from the UserModel that pulls in the email field from the auth_identities table. 

class UserModel extends ShieldUsers implements CustomRecyclerQuery
{
    public function setupRecycler(): static
    {
        return $this->select("users.*, 
            (SELECT secret 
                from auth_identities 
                where user_id = users.id
                    and type = 'email_password'
                order by last_used_at desc 
                limit 1
            ) as email
       ");
    }
}

docs.title: Overriding the Restore
docs.text:
You may override the default handling of the restore process if you have needs outside simply setting the deleted_at date to null. Implement CustomRecyclerRestore and its recyclerRestore() method. It only accepts a single argument, the record primary key, and returns whether the record was restored. 

public function recyclerRestore(int $id): bool
{
    return $this->where('id', $id)
        ->set('deleted_at', null)
        ->update();
}

docs.title: Overriding the Purge
docs.text:
You may override the default handling of the purge process if you have needs outside simply deleting the record. Implement CustomRecyclerPurge and its recyclerPurge() method. It only accepts a single argument, the record primary key, and returns whether the record was purged.

public function recyclerPurge(int $id): bool
{
    return (bool) $this->delete($id, true);
}

docs.title: Resource Tabs
docs.text:
Resource tabs are the tabs shown when editing a resource: a single User or User Group. They let your module add its own tab to those pages without editing Bonfire's views.

Two resources accept tabs:

Resource Page Shown to users with user admin/users/{id} access to the page group admin/settings/groups/{alias} groups.edit

docs.title: Registering a tab
docs.text:
Add the tab from the initAdmin() method of your module's Module.php. A tab needs a title, the URL it links to and, optionally, a permission:

use Bonfire\Resources\ResourceTab;

public function initAdmin()
{
    service('resourceTabs')->addTabFor('user', new ResourceTab([
        'title'      => 'Notes',
        'url'        => 'users/(id)/notes',
        'permission' => 'users.edit',
    ]));
}
  • title is the text on the tab.
  • url is relative to the admin area: ADMIN_AREA is put in front of it. Write (id) where the ID of the resource being edited goes. It is read from the current URL, so on /admin/users/123 the tab above links to /admin/users/123/notes. For groups, the ID is the group's alias, such as admin.
  • permission, if set, hides the tab from users who don't have that permission.

The tab is shown as the current one when the page's URL matches its link.

docs.title: Building the tab's page
docs.text:
The tab only links to a page; your module provides that page. Add a route for it in your module's Config/Routes.php:

$routes->group(ADMIN_AREA, ['namespace' => '\App\Modules\Notes\Controllers'], static function ($routes) {
    $routes->get('users/(:num)/notes', 'NotesController::index/$1');
});

Then a controller that loads the user and renders a view:

namespace App\Modules\Notes\Controllers;

use Bonfire\Core\AdminController;
use Bonfire\Users\Models\UserModel;

class NotesController extends AdminController
{
    public function index(int $userId)
    {
        if (! auth()->user()->can('users.edit')) {
            return redirect()->to(ADMIN_AREA)->with('error', lang('Bonfire.notAuthorized'));
        }

        $user = model(UserModel::class)->find($userId);
        if ($user === null) {
            return redirect()->back()->with('error', lang('Bonfire.resourceNotFound', [lang('Users.userGenitive')]));
        }

        return $this->render('App\Modules\Notes\Views\notes', ['user' => $user]);
    }
}

Check the permission in the controller too: the tab's permission only hides the link, it doesn't protect the page.

In the view, include the user's header and tab bar so your page looks like the other tabs. Pass tab a name that none of Bonfire's tabs use, so only your tab is marked as current:

<?php $this->extend('master') ?>

<?php $this->section('main') ?>
<?= $this->include('Bonfire\Users\Views\_user_head') ?>

<?= view('Bonfire\Users\Views\_tabs', ['tab' => 'notes', 'user' => $user]) ?>

<x-admin-box title="Notes">
    ...
</x-admin-box>
<?php $this->endSection() ?>

For a group tab, include Bonfire\Groups\Views\_tabs instead. It needs title (shown in the page header), group (the group's alias) and tab.

docs.title: Search
docs.text: Bonfire provides a flexible search system that is highlighted on all areas of the admin area. In order to make this as powerful as possible, any module may integrate into the search results, both by adding filters for the Advanced Search form, and by providing results that will be displayed.

docs.title: Providing Search Results
docs.text:
The most basic integration is to register your module as a search provider. This is done by creating a class at the root of your module's code called SearchProvider. It must extend Bonfire\Search\Interfaces\SearchProviderInterface and fill in a few small methods. Below is an example search provider for module Users.

<?php

namespace Bonfire\Users;

use Bonfire\Search\Interfaces\SearchProviderInterface;
use Bonfire\Users\Models\UserModel;

class SearchProvider extends UserModel implements SearchProviderInterface
{
    /**
     * Performs a primary search for just this resource.
     *
     * @param string     $term
     * @param int        $limit
     * @param array|null $post
     *
     * @return array
     */
    public function search(string $term, int $limit = 10, ?array $post = null): array
    {
        return $this->select('users.*')
            ->distinct()
            ->join('auth_identities', 'auth_identities.user_id = users.id', 'inner')
            ->like('first_name', $term, 'right', true, true)
            ->orlike('last_name', $term, 'right', true, true)
            ->orLike('username', $term, 'right', true, true)
            ->orLike('secret', $term, 'both', true, true)
            ->orderBy('first_name', 'asc')
            ->findAll($limit);
    }

    /**
     * Returns the name of the resource.
     *
     * @return string
     */
    public function resourceName(): string
    {
        return 'users';
    }

    /**
     * Returns a URL to the admin area URL main list
     * for this resource.
     *
     * @return string
     */
    public function resourceUrl(): string
    {
        return ADMIN_AREA .'/users';
    }

    /**
     * Returns the name of the view to use when
     * displaying the list of results for this
     * resource type.
     *
     * @return string
     */
    public function resultView(): string
    {
        return 'Search/users';
    }
}

search()

Given the search term it will return an array of any search results for this resource type. You'll see this SearcProvider extends the UserModel. It is not necessary to do so, but is a simple way to get access to the model features when you need them.

If you want the search to find not only the data from the main table, but also the related meta info (see Meta Info), you should:

  1. Put a property $includeMetaFieldsInSearch into the module config file (example for app/Config/Users.php, since, suppose, we want to be able to search for users by their blog urls, which we keep in the meta_info table):

        public $includeMetaFieldsInSearch = [
    'blog',
    ];

  2. Employ Bonfire\Core\Traits\SearchInMeta trait: put use Bonfire\Core\Traits\SearchInMeta; before the SearchProvider class declaration and use SearchInMeta after the class declaration;

  3. Write the search() method employing the trait methods joinMetaInfo and orLikeInMetaInfo() when constructing the query:

    public function search(string $term, int $limit = 10, ?array $post = null): array
{
    $query = $this->select('users.*')->distinct();
    $query->join('auth_identities', 'auth_identities.user_id = users.id', 'inner');

    $searchInMeta = setting('Users.includeMetaFieldsInSearch');

    if (!empty($searchInMeta)) {
        // first argument is the resource entity name, second – the DB table name
        $query->joinMetaInfo('Bonfire\Users\User', 'users');
    }

    $query->like('first_name', $term, 'right', true, true)
        ->orlike('last_name', $term, 'right', true, true)
        ->orLike('username', $term, 'right', true, true)
        ->orLike('secret', $term, 'both', true, true);

    if (!empty($searchInMeta)) {
        foreach ($searchInMeta as $metaField) {
            // here syntax almost exactly like that of orLike()
            $query->orLikeInMetaInfo($metaField, $term, 'both', true, true);
        }
    }

    $query->orderBy('first_name', 'asc');

    return $query->findAll($limit);
}

resourceName()

The name of the resource. This is displayed as a header on the search results page where it shows the top 10 results from all search providers.

resourceUrl()

Returns the relative URL to the main page for this resource. In this case it takes you to the list of users.

resultView()

Returns the name of the view that should be used to display the results on the overview page. This MUST be in the Admin theme folder in order to be found. This can be a fairly straight-forward view file:

<table class="table table-hover">
    <?= $this->setData(['headers' => [
        'email' => 'Email',
        'username' => 'Username',
        'groups' => 'Groups',
        'last_active' => 'Last Active'
    ]])->include('_table_head') ?>
    <tbody>
    <?php service('actions')->for('users')->showing($rows) ?>
    <?php foreach($rows as $user) : ?>
        <tr>
            <?= view('Bonfire\Users\Views\_row_info', ['user' => $user]) ?>
        </tr>
    <?php endforeach ?>
    </tbody>
</table>

docs.title: Tutorial: Build Your First Admin Module
docs.text:
In this tutorial you will build a Blog module that adds a Posts screen to the admin area. By the end you will have:

  • a "Posts" item in the sidebar, shown only to groups that may use it
  • a paginated list of posts built from the admin theme's components
  • a search box and a status filter that update the list without reloading the page
  • posts in the admin's global search results
  • deleted posts in the Recycler, ready to be restored

Every step ends with something to check in your browser before you move on.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
You need:

  • a CodeIgniter 4 app with Bonfire installed (see Installation)
  • the app running, for example with php spark serve, and a superadmin account you can log in with
  • some familiarity with CodeIgniter routes, controllers, models and migrations

All paths below are relative to your project root.

docs.title: Step 1: Turn on module discovery
docs.text:
Bonfire only finds modules in folders listed in Config\Bonfire::$appModules. The entry for app/Modules ships commented out. Open app/Config/Bonfire.php and uncomment it:

public $appModules = [
    'App\Modules' => APPPATH . 'Modules',
];

Now create the folders for the Blog module:

app/
    Modules/
        Blog/
            Config/
            Controllers/
            Database/
                Migrations/
                Seeds/
            Models/
            Views/

Every class in the module lives in the App\Modules\Blog namespace.

Check it: nothing changes in the browser yet. Bonfire only loads a module once it has a Module.php, which you will add in step 3. Bonfire caches the module folders it finds for a minute, so if Blog doesn't show up then, run php spark cache:clear.

docs.title: Step 2: Create the posts table
docs.text:
The list needs data. Create a migration at app/Modules/Blog/Database/Migrations/2026-10-29-120000_CreatePostsTable.php:

<?php

namespace App\Modules\Blog\Database\Migrations;

use CodeIgniter\Database\Migration;

class CreatePostsTable extends Migration
{
    public function up()
    {
        $this->forge->addField([
            'id'         => ['type' => 'int', 'unsigned' => true, 'auto_increment' => true],
            'title'      => ['type' => 'varchar', 'constraint' => 200],
            'status'     => ['type' => 'varchar', 'constraint' => 20, 'default' => 'draft'],
            'created_at' => ['type' => 'datetime', 'null' => true],
            'updated_at' => ['type' => 'datetime', 'null' => true],
            'deleted_at' => ['type' => 'datetime', 'null' => true],
        ]);
        $this->forge->addPrimaryKey('id');
        $this->forge->createTable('posts');
    }

    public function down()
    {
        $this->forge->dropTable('posts');
    }
}

The deleted_at column lets the model soft-delete posts, which the Recycler needs in step 9.

Then a seeder at app/Modules/Blog/Database/Seeds/PostSeeder.php that adds a few posts. The last one is already deleted, so you will have something to find in the Recycler later:

<?php

namespace App\Modules\Blog\Database\Seeds;

use CodeIgniter\Database\Seeder;
use CodeIgniter\I18n\Time;

class PostSeeder extends Seeder
{
    public function run()
    {
        $now   = Time::now()->toDateTimeString();
        $posts = [
            ['Hello, world', 'published'],
            ['Why we moved to CodeIgniter 4', 'published'],
            ['Ten tips for faster pages', 'published'],
            ['Our roadmap for next year', 'draft'],
            ['Behind the scenes', 'draft'],
            ['Meet the team', 'published'],
            ['A post nobody needs', 'draft', $now],
        ];

        foreach ($posts as $post) {
            $this->db->table('posts')->insert([
                'title'      => $post[0],
                'status'     => $post[1],
                'created_at' => $now,
                'updated_at' => $now,
                'deleted_at' => $post[2] ?? null,
            ]);
        }
    }
}

Run both:

php spark migrate --all
php spark db:seed "App\Modules\Blog\Database\Seeds\PostSeeder"

Check it: php spark db:table posts shows seven posts, the last with a deleted_at date.

docs.title: Step 3: Add a menu item
docs.text:
A module joins the admin through its Module.php. Bonfire calls its initAdmin() method on every admin page, and that is where you add the module's menu items. Create app/Modules/Blog/Module.php:

<?php

namespace App\Modules\Blog;

use Bonfire\Core\BaseModule;
use Bonfire\Menus\MenuItem;

class Module extends BaseModule
{
    public function initAdmin()
    {
        $item = new MenuItem([
            'title'           => 'Posts',
            'namedRoute'      => 'posts-list',
            'fontAwesomeIcon' => 'fas fa-newspaper',
        ]);
        service('menus')->menu('sidebar')->collection('content')->addItem($item);
    }
}

The item goes in the sidebar's content collection, next to Users. A menu item links to a named route, so define posts-list in app/Modules/Blog/Config/Routes.php:

<?php

$routes->group(ADMIN_AREA, ['namespace' => 'App\Modules\Blog\Controllers'], static function ($routes) {
    $routes->get('posts', 'PostController::list', ['as' => 'posts-list']);
});

ADMIN_AREA is the admin's URL prefix, admin by default, so the list lives at /admin/posts.
