docs.title: Bonfire Modules
docs.text: Bonfire provides several powerful modules to help you build and manage your web applications efficiently. Below is an overview of the main modules available in Bonfire.

docs.title: Asset Management
docs.text:
Bonfire provides a simple assets system that allows you to serve CSS/JS assets from anywhere, handle browser caching, and cache-busting with updated assets.

Read more about Asset Management

docs.title: Authentication and Authorization
docs.text:
All authentication and authorization in Bonfire are handled by CodeIgniter's Shield library. This library provides a flexible and powerful system for managing users, groups, and permissions.

Read more about Authentication and Authorization

docs.title: Meta Info
docs.text:
Bonfire provides Entity-Attribute-Value style storage for additional data of entities used with your models. By default it can be used to add meta information to users, and it can be adapted to store meta information for the entities managed by your own admin modules. While not exactly a module but a set of core traits, it can be tapped into accross your application.

Read more about Meta Info

docs.title: Consent
docs.text:
The Consent module helps you manage collecting consent from users before storing any cookies through an opt-in system for all non-required cookies.

Read more about Consent

docs.title: Dashboard
docs.text:
The Dashboard is the first page you see when you log into the admin area. It provides a place to put widgets that offer a quick overview of the site's status or other important information.

Read more about the Dashboard

docs.title: Users
docs.text:
The Users module lists the people who can log in, and lets you add, edit, ban and delete them, change their groups and permissions, and set the rules for registration, passwords and avatars.

Read more about Users

docs.title: Groups
docs.text: The Groups module, under Settings → Groups, lists the user groups and sets which permissions each group grants.

docs.title: General Settings
docs.text:
The General settings screen holds the site's name, whether it's online, the admin's accent color, and the timezone and date formats.

Read more about General Settings

docs.title: Email
docs.text:
The Email settings screen controls how the site sends email: the sender's name and address, and the SMTP, Mail or Sendmail delivery details.

Read more about Email Settings

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
The Tools module adds System Info, a summary of the server and its writable folders, and a viewer for the site's log files.

Read more about Tools

docs.title: Recycler
docs.text:
The Recycler, under Tools, holds records that were deleted, such as users, so you can restore them or delete them for good.

Read more about the Recycler

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
The Actions module runs the row and bulk actions in admin lists, such as deleting users, and adds a dashboard widget showing recent action runs.

Read more about Actions

docs.title: Asset Management
docs.text:
Bonfire provides a simple assets system that was created to solve two main challenges:

  1. We should be able to serve CSS/JS assets from anywhere. While this is primarily for use by themes, it could serve many purposes.
  2. How to easily handle browser caching/cache-busting with updated assets.

And try to do this in the simplest way possible.

For the examples, we will link to assets for the Admin theme. To add assets to your own site theme step by step, see Add CSS and JS to Your Site Theme.

Warning

To make this all work, a route is specified at /assets/(:any) to capture the request. The assets system will not work if you override this route in your own application. For most sites this should not be a problem.

docs.title: Loading the Helpers
docs.text:
As long as you use Bonfire's custom View system, this helper will be automatically loaded. Otherwise, you will need to load it manually.

helper('assets');

docs.title: Defining Asset Locations
docs.text:
The first step is to define the locations where assets can be located. This is done in the app/Config/Assets.php file, which php spark bf:install publishes. The $folders array defines an alias for each folder that we can reference later, and the actual path to the folder.

public $folders = [
    'app' => ROOTPATH.'themes/App',
    'admin' => ROOTPATH.'themes/Admin',
    'auth' => ROOTPATH.'themes/Auth',
    'other' => ROOTPATH.'vendor',
];

docs.title: Linking to assets
docs.text: Within your views you can link to assets anywhere within your project with the asset() or asset_link() helper functions.

docs.title: asset_link()
docs.text:
asset_link() takes up to three arguments. The first is the path to the file to load. The first segment of this path must be one of the defined folders. The rest of the path would be based on the actual file structure within that location.

{$folder alias}/path/to/file.{css|js}

For the Admin theme, a folder has been defined called admin. Both the Auth and App themes have similar folders already defined. Assuming there was a file at themes/Admin/css/admin.css, you would build the link to it like this:

'admin/css/admin.css'

The second argument is the type of asset being loaded. This tells it how the resulting link should be formed. Currently, it only supports css and js files.

<?= asset_link('admin/css/admin.css', 'css') ?>
<?= asset_link('admin/js/admin.js', 'js') ?>

The optional third argument adds attributes to the tag. Pass a string for a value-less attribute, or an array of name/value pairs. CSS links get rel='stylesheet' unless your array sets its own rel.

<?= asset_link('admin/js/admin.js', 'js', 'defer') ?>
<?= asset_link('admin/css/print.css', 'css', ['media' => 'print']) ?>

docs.title: asset()
docs.text:
The asset() function is similar, except it only returns the URL and allows you to include it in your own HTML tags manually if needed.

<link rel="stylesheet" href="<?= asset('admin/css/admin.css', 'css') ?>" />
<script src="<?= asset('admin/js/admin.js', 'js') ?>"></script>

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: The Config\Assets class has a handful of settings to customize the experience.

docs.title: $bustingType
docs.text:
When a link is generated it includes a string within the filename for cache-busting reasons. This would look something like: https://localhost:8080/assets/admin/css/admin~~213264216523.css. The config setting, $bustingType defines how this string is derived. It has two possible values, either file or version.

The file setting will examine the requested file and use the file modified date/time as the basis, and convert it to a Unix timestamp. This is the easiest value to use as it is automatically updates itself based on the file. However, it does force an extra file read, and the overhead needed to get the information from the file. On many small to medium sites this is likely just fine. However, large sites, or sites that require every ounce of performance, may want to use the version method.

The version method requires the developer to set a new version in the configuration file whenever new code is ready to deploy to staging or production environments. See the next setting for details. To make this easier during development the current timestamp is used in testing/development environments ensuring that no caching will happen. In other environments it inserts the version number that was specified.

docs.title: $separator
docs.text: The $separator setting allows the app to detect the part of the asset file name that was added for cache-busting purposes. It can be a single web-safe non-reserved character or a combination of such characters (characters that are allowed in a URI, but do not have a reserved purpose) that DOES NOT OCCUR in your asset file names (like ~, - or _ or any combination of ASCII letters and numbers). The default is ~~. Separator will be inserted before the file version/timestamp, in between the file name and file extension.

docs.title: $versions
docs.text:
The $versions setting allows you to define the version number for css and js separately. This value is used as the cache-busting string when the version busting type is used.

public $versions = [
    'css' => '1.0',
    'js' => '1.0',
];

docs.title: $folders
docs.text:
This value is where you define the folders that are searched when linking to an asset. Folders for all themes and the vendor folder are setup by default.

public $folders = [
    'app' => ROOTPATH.'themes/App',
    'admin' => ROOTPATH.'themes/Admin',
    'auth' => ROOTPATH.'themes/Auth',
    'other' => ROOTPATH.'vendor',
];

docs.title: Authentication and Authorization
docs.text:
All of the authentication and authorization is handled by CodeIgniter's Shield library. This library provides a flexible and powerful system for managing users, groups, and permissions. Please refer to the Shield documentation for more information on how to use it.

Bonfire ships its own Auth config, Bonfire\Auth\Config\Auth, which extends Shield's. This page lists the defaults that decide how login and registration behave, and the components the auth pages are built from. For every other key, see the Configuration Reference.

docs.title: Bonfire's Defaults
docs.text: Key Default Effect Change it in $allowRegistration true Visitors can create their own account at /register, and the login page links to it. When false, the register page sends visitors back with an error and only an admin can add users. Settings → Users or code $allowMagicLinkLogins true Users who forgot their password can ask for a one-time login link by email at /login/magic-link. The login page links to it. When false, the link is hidden and the magic link pages refuse requests. Code $magicLinkLifetime HOUR How long, in seconds, a magic link works. Code $actions['register'] null Nothing happens after registration; the new user is logged in. See Actions. Settings → Users or code $actions['login'] null Nothing happens after login. See Actions. Settings → Users or code $redirects See Redirects Where users go after login, logout, registration and denied access. Code

docs.title: Redirects
docs.text:
Key Default When it's used login '/' After a successful login. logout 'login' After logout. register '/' After registration, and after email activation. force_reset '/' When a user's account is flagged for a forced password reset. permission_denied '/' When a user lacks a permission a route filter requires. group_denied '/' When a user isn't in a group a route filter requires.

Each value can be an absolute URL (https://example.com), a named route, or a URI path (account).

Users with the admin.access permission ignore login: after login they always go to the admin area. Everyone else goes back to the page they were on when they were asked to log in, or to login if there wasn't one. To change this, override loginRedirect() in your app/Config/Auth.php.

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
An action is an extra step Shield runs after login or registration, before the user gets in. Both are off by default. Bonfire has its own version of each of Shield's two email actions. They render their pages with the Auth theme, so use them instead of Shield's.

Key Class What the user sees Settings → Users switch register Bonfire\Auth\Actions\EmailActivator After registering, they get a code by email and must enter it to activate their account. Force email verification login Bonfire\Auth\Actions\Email2FA After entering their password, they get a code by email and must enter it to finish logging in. Force 2FA after login

Both actions send email, so set up Email first.

The switches recognize only Bonfire's classes. If you set Shield's classes, or your own, in code, the switch shows as off, and saving the screen replaces your class with null.

docs.title: Changing a Default
docs.text: You can change a default in three places. A value stored in the database wins over the config file.

docs.title: On the Settings → Users screen
docs.text: Admins with the users.settings permission can change registration, the two actions, remember-me and the password rules under Settings → Users. The screen saves each value with setting(), so it is stored in the database.

docs.title: In app/Config/Auth.php
docs.text:
The installer publishes app/Config/Auth.php, a copy of Bonfire's Auth config with every key in it. Edit a value there to change the default for every environment. For example, to turn off magic links and send users to an account page after login and registration:

public bool $allowMagicLinkLogins = false;

public array $redirects = [
    'register'          => 'account',
    'login'             => 'account',
    'logout'            => 'login',
    'force_reset'       => '/',
    'permission_denied' => '/',
    'group_denied'      => '/',
];

Keep every key of $redirects, even the ones you don't change. Bonfire reads each one, so a missing key causes an error.

docs.title: With setting()
docs.text:
To change a value from code at runtime, such as in a migration or a seeder, store it with setting():

setting('Auth.allowMagicLinkLogins', false);

Warning

Once a key is stored in the database, Bonfire reads it from there and ignores app/Config/Auth.php. This happens the first time an admin saves Settings → Users, which stores allowRegistration and actions. Changing those keys in the config file afterwards has no effect. Remove the stored value to go back to the config file:

setting()->forget('Auth.allowRegistration');

See Settings for how stored settings work.

docs.title: Extending the Authentication System
docs.text: While none of the functionality has been overridden, the views and controllers have been extended to integrate with Bonfire's theme system. This allows you to easily customize the look and feel of the authentication system to match the rest of your application.

docs.title: Views
docs.text:
The authentication pages are styled via the auth theme. Much of the look and feel can be modified by modifying the theme itself. If you need to modify the forms or other elements, you can specify the view that should be used in the Auth configuration file and then create your own views.

public array $views = [
    'layout'                      => 'master',
    'email_layout'                => '\Bonfire\Views\email',
    'login'                       => '\Bonfire\Views\Auth\login',
    'register'                    => '\Bonfire\Views\Auth\register',
    'forgotPassword'              => '\CodeIgniter\Shield\Views\forgot_password',
    'resetPassword'               => '\CodeIgniter\Shield\Views\reset_password',
    'action_email_2fa'            => '\Bonfire\Views\Auth\email_2fa_show',
    'action_email_2fa_verify'     => '\Bonfire\Views\Auth\email_2fa_verify',
    'action_email_2fa_email'      => '\CodeIgniter\Shield\Views\Email\email_2fa_email',
    'action_email_activate_show'  => '\Bonfire\Views\Auth\email_activate_show',
    'action_email_activate_email' => '\CodeIgniter\Shield\Views\Email\email_activate_email',
    'magic-link-login'            => '\Bonfire\Views\Auth\magic_link_form',
    'magic-link-message'          => '\Bonfire\Views\Auth\magic_link_message',
    'magic-link-email'            => '\Bonfire\Views\Auth\magic_link_email',
];

You can change the main layout that is used for the authentication pages by changing the layout value. You can change the layout used for emails by changing the email_layout value.

docs.title: Controllers
docs.text:
When you need to modify the behavior of the authentication system, you should create a new controller and extend the existing controller. You should then override only the methods that you need to modify. If possible, you should do your changes and call the parent method to ensure that any security fixes that are discovered later are not lost to your application due to your overrides.

namespace App\Controllers\Auth;

use Bonfire\Auth\Controllers\LoginController as BonfireLoginController;

class LoginController extends BonfireLoginController
{
    // ... your custom methods here
}

Info

You should always extend the Bonfire controller, not the Shield controller. This will ensure that the theme system is used properly, as Bonfire's auth controllers extend the view methods to use the theme system.

docs.title: Auth Theme Components
docs.text: The Auth theme has two view components of its own. Bonfire's login, register, email 2FA, email activation and magic link views are built from them. The installer publishes them to themes/Auth/Components/, so you can edit them there to change every auth page at once.

docs.title: <x-auth-card>
docs.text:
A Bootstrap card for an auth form. It is slightly transparent, so the page background shows through, and it is 5 columns wide on large screens and 7 on medium ones. It has no attributes; put the card's content in its slot.

<x-auth-card>
    <div class="card-body">
        <h5 class="card-title mb-5">Log in</h5>
        <!-- form -->
    </div>
</x-auth-card>

docs.title: <x-unsplash>
docs.text:
A full-screen photo behind the page content. It has no attributes; put the page content in its slot. It loads a random photo from Picsum and shows an "Image by Picsum" credit in the bottom-right corner. Despite the component's name, the photo doesn't come from Unsplash.

Because the photo comes from an external site, every visitor's browser requests it from picsum.photos. To use your own image, or a plain background, edit themes/Auth/Components/unsplash.php.

docs.title: Using them together
docs.text:
Bonfire's auth views put the card inside the background, in a centered container:

<x-unsplash>
    <div class="container d-flex justify-content-center p-5">
        <x-auth-card>
            <div class="card-body">
                <!-- form -->
            </div>
        </x-auth-card>
    </div>
</x-unsplash>

docs.title: Consent
docs.text:
With the Global Data Protection Regulation and other data privacy regulations being put in place across the globe, you have various requirements as web developers that you didn't use to. The Consent module helps you manage collecting consent from the user before storing any cookies through an opt-in system for all non-required cookies. It provides the mechanism for displaying the consent form, and recording the user's preferences.

For a step-by-step example, see Load Analytics Only After Visitors Consent.

docs.title: Defining the Consent Types
docs.text:
The Consent module allows you to define the types of consent that you would like to collect from the user. These are defined in the Config\Consent class. The default consents are:

public array $consents = [
    'required' => [
        'name' => 'Functionality',
        'desc' => 'These cookies are required for the normal operation of this website.',
    ],
    'performance' => [
        'name' => 'Performance',
        'desc' => 'These cookies help us measure how visitors use the site, what the traffic sources are,
            and which pages are popular. This helps to improve the website for everyone. If you reject these
            we will be unable to use your visits to make site improvements.',
    ],
    'targeting' => [
        'name' => 'Targeting',
        'desc' => 'These are usually placed by third-party advertising networks, which may use information about
            your visits to develop a profile of your interests. This information may be shared with other networks
            or sites to deliver more relevant advertising across multiple sites.',
    ],
];

docs.title: Using the Helper
docs.text:
A helper method, has_consent, is provided so that you can easily meet the consent requirements when building your site.

The helper is loaded automatically by the BaseController. As long as you extend the BaseController (or one of its children, like the AuthController) then you do not need to explicitly load the helper.

The helper can be used both within the views and the controllers to limit which services are called (like ad-tracking or analytics) and which cookies you set.

Pass the consent's key from $consents. Within a view you might wrap a Google Analytics tag within a check against the performance consent:

<?php if (has_consent('performance')) : ?>
<script>
    <!-- Global Site Tag (gtag.js) - Google Analytics -->
    ... (several lines of code) ...
</script>
<?php endif ?>

docs.title: Customizing the Consent Form
docs.text:
The consent form is a view that can be customized to fit your site's design. The view can be changed by editing the Consent config file:

public string $consentForm = 'Bonfire\Consent\Views\consent_form';

You can also specify the CSS and Javascript files that are loaded with the form:

public string $consentFormStyles  = 'Bonfire\Consent\Views\consent_styles';
public string $consentFormScripts = 'Bonfire\Consent\Views\consent_scripts';

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
All settings are available in the Config\Consent class. Everything except the form views can also be changed in the admin area under Settings → Consent, which saves the values to the database.

$requireConsent

This determines whether the consent system is enabled or not. If true, the consent form will be automatically inserted into all front-end views by the Consent controller filter. If false, the consent system will not display and the helper will always return true. The default value is false;

$consentLength

The number of days before a visitor is asked for their consent again. The default value is 180 days (6 months).

$consentForm

The view that is displayed to site visitors that a) asks for their basic consent and b) allows them to accept/reject the various consents. The required consent is unable to be rejected and contains things like the Auth cookie that determines if you're logged in or not.

$consentFormStyles $consentFormScripts

The views that will be loaded that contain the CSS and Javascript, respectively. The contents of these views will be inserted into each page upon page load.

$policyUrl

A URL (either full or relative) that points to the page that details the cookie policy. On many sites this will be included in the Privacy Policy or Terms of Service pages, or similar. The default value is privacy.

$policyTitle

The link text used for the cookie policy link in the consent form. The default value is Cookie Policy.

$consentMessage

The message shown to visitors at the top of the consent form. Put {policy_url} where the cookie policy link should appear; it is replaced with a link to $policyUrl that uses $policyTitle as its text.

$consents

This is an array of the initial consents that will be asked for in the Consent Form. Each array item includes the alias the consent can be checked with, and the following items:

  • name: The name as it is displayed to the visitors.
  • desc: The description of the consent that describes the purpose of the cookies/services and what might be no longer functional if the consent is rejected.

docs.title: The Dashboard
docs.text:
The Dashboard is the first page you see when you log into the admin area. It holds widgets that give a quick overview of the site's status, or other information that is important to you.

Every admin can arrange their own dashboard without changing anyone else's. Until they do, they see the site default. To write a widget of your own, see Dashboard Widgets.

docs.title: Customizing your dashboard
docs.text:
Click Customize to enter edit mode. Nothing is stored until you click Save layout; Cancel puts the dashboard back the way it was. Every change can be undone and redone with the arrows in the edit bar, or Ctrl+Z (⌘Z) and Shift+Ctrl+Z, and the message after a removal or deletion has its own Undo.

In edit mode you can:

  • drag a widget to reorder it, also into another section;
  • change a widget's settings from its sliders button, when it has any;
  • remove a widget with its trash button;
  • reset to the site default with the clock button. Saving the site default as your layout forgets yours, so you follow the site default again when a site admin changes it.

docs.title: Sections
docs.text: A layout is a list of sections, each with an optional heading. From a section's ⋯ menu you can add a widget to it, move it up or down, insert a section below it, or delete it along with its widgets. Sections left without widgets are dropped on save, and a layout holds at most 20 sections.

docs.title: Sizes
docs.text: Size a widget from the tools above it, or drag its bottom-right corner. The sizes are ¼, ⅓, ½, ⅔ and Full width (3, 4, 6, 8 or 12 of 12 columns), within the range that widget allows. Quick Links is always full width.

docs.title: The widget library
docs.text: Add widget opens the library. It lists every widget available to you, grouped by the module that adds it, and marks the ones already on your dashboard. Click Add, or drag one straight onto a section. An added widget shows a placeholder until you save.

docs.title: Keyboard and screen readers
docs.text:
Every edit also works from the keyboard. With a widget focused:

Key Does Arrow keys Move it. Up and Down, and Left and Right past either end, move it to the section before or after. Shift + Left / Right Resize it. Delete Remove it.

Screen readers hear each change announced.

docs.title: Widget settings
docs.text:
A widget's sliders button opens its settings in the panel on the right, with the widget outlined on the dashboard. The settings are your own: they change that widget on your dashboard only. Apply keeps them as part of your edit, so undo, Cancel and Save layout cover them like any other change, and the widget shows Changes apply on save until you save. A widget you just added can be set up before you save, too.

Until you change a setting, it uses the widget's default. Once you change it, yours is kept. Reset to defaults fills the panel with the widget's defaults again. Widgets without settings, such as Quick Links, have no sliders button.

Widget Settings Stat cards Show the "View Detail" link Line chart Show the title, Show the legend, Legend position, Enable animation, Line tension Bar, doughnut, pie and polar area charts Show the title, Show the legend, Legend position, Enable animation, Color scheme Log activity Days to show, Hide Debug entries Users by group Sort by most users first or by group name Newest users Users to show (1–10) Recent failed logins Attempts to show (1–20) Recently active Active within (5 minutes, 1 hour, 24 hours), Users to show (1–10) Action runs Runs to show (1–20), Days to show (1–30), Include completed runs Recent errors Entries to show (1–20), Show errors only or errors and warnings System health Warn when server load is above (0.5–100)

Save as site default carries each widget's settings into the site default.

docs.title: Built-in widgets
docs.text:
A widget's permission decides who may use it. Admins who lack it don't see it in their library or on their dashboard, its data is never fetched for them, and it is dropped from any layout they save. A widget that becomes available later shows up in the library of admins who have customized, never in their layout.

Widget Shows Permission Default layout Quick Links A greeting, and a link to each item of the sidebar's Content section you may see. none Yes Users by group Each group, a bar scaled to the largest one, and its number of users. users.list Yes, in Users Newest users The latest users to join, linking to each. users.list Yes, in Users Recently active The users active within the last 5 minutes, hour or 24 hours, most recent first, with how long ago, linking to each. Users who have never been active don't appear. users.list No Users in Recycler A stat card counting deleted users, linking to them in the Recycler. users.list No Recent failed logins The newest unsuccessful login attempts across all accounts: who tried, from which IP address, and when. An attempt whose email belongs to a user links to that user's Security tab, for admins who may open it. users.view No User Groups A stat card counting the groups, linking to the group settings. groups.settings No Log activity One stacked bar per day up to today, split into Error, Warning, Info and Debug entries, with a thin line for days without a log file. CRITICAL, ALERT and EMERGENCY count as Error, NOTICE as Info. Each bar links to that log file, and the headline counts the errors across the days shown. logs.view Yes, in Monitoring Recent errors The newest errors, or errors and warnings, across the log files, linking to each log file. logs.view Yes, in Monitoring System health What is wrong with the install, if anything: each file or folder in writable/ that can't be written to, a missing .env file, and a 1-minute server load above Warn when server load is above (default 4). With no problems it says so in one line. Links to the System Info page. admin.settings No Recycler Each resource in the Recycler that has deleted records, with how many, linking to its list. When the Recycler is empty it says so in one line. recycler.view No Action runs Your own queued bulk action runs that need attention: queued and running runs, plus runs that failed in the last Days to show. Turn on Include completed runs to list finished runs too. Each row links to the run's progress page. none: admins only see the runs they started No

Widgets marked No are added from the widget library.

docs.title: The site default
docs.text:
Admins who have not saved their own layout see the site default. The dashboard picks the first of these that exists:

  1. the admin's own saved layout;
  2. the site default saved with Save as site default;
  3. the $layout of the Dashboard config file, or, when that is null, the cells of $cells in order (see Legacy: view cells).

docs.title: Saving it from the dashboard
docs.text:
Admins with the widgets.settings permission get Save as site default in the edit bar. It stores the layout as shown as the site default, which every admin without their own layout then sees, and forgets the saver's own layout so they follow it too. Other admins who customized keep theirs. Widgets the saver may not see aren't in their editor, so they aren't in the saved default either.

Reset site default, next to it in the edit bar, forgets the stored site default, so it goes back to the configured $layout. It asks first. Admins' own layouts are kept.

docs.title: Setting it in config
docs.text:
Out of the box, the site default is the $layout property of the Dashboard config file:

  • the quick links;
  • a Users section with Users by group and Newest users, each half the width;
  • a Monitoring section with Log activity and Recent errors, each half the width.
public ?array $layout = [
    'version'  => 1,
    'sections' => [
        ['title' => '', 'widgets' => [
            ['id' => 'cell:Bonfire\Dashboard\DashboardCells::quickLinks', 'size' => 'full'],
        ]],
        ['title' => 'Users', 'widgets' => [
            ['id' => 'users:byGroup', 'size' => 'half'],
            ['id' => 'users:newest', 'size' => 'half'],
        ]],
        ['title' => 'Monitoring', 'widgets' => [
            ['id' => 'logs:logActivity', 'size' => 'half'],
            ['id' => 'tools:recentErrors', 'size' => 'half'],
        ]],
    ],
];

Change it to give every admin without their own layout, while no site default is saved, a different one. Each entry is a widget's id and its size (quarter, third, half, two-thirds or full). Widgets the viewer may not see are left out, and so is a section left empty.

docs.title: Email Settings
docs.text:
The Email settings screen controls how your site sends email, such as password resets, email verification codes and two-factor login codes. Open Email under Settings in the sidebar. You need the admin.settings permission.

Change what you need, then click Save Settings.

docs.title: Set up SMTP
docs.text:
Most email providers, such as Mailgun, Postmark, Amazon SES or your web host, give you SMTP details to send through.

  1. Under From, enter the name and address your emails come from. Use an address your provider lets you send from.
  2. Under Delivery, choose SMTP.
  3. Enter the Host, Username and Password your provider gave you.

  4. Choose the Port and Encryption your provider asks for. The usual pairs are:

    Port Encryption 587 TLS 465 SSL 25 or 2525 None or TLS

    If your provider uses another port, choose other and type it in.

  5. Click Save Settings.

To check the settings, send yourself an email from the site, for example with "forgot password" on the login page.

docs.title: From
docs.text: Setting What it does Name The sender name emails show, such as your site's name. Required, at least 2 characters. Email The address emails are sent from. Required.

docs.title: Delivery
docs.text:
Setting What it does Protocol How mail is sent: SMTP through a mail server, Mail through PHP's mail() function, or Sendmail through the server's sendmail program. Sendmail path Where the sendmail program is, such as /usr/sbin/sendmail. Shown for Sendmail.

Mail has no options of its own and only works on Linux servers that are set up to send mail.

docs.title: SMTP
docs.text:
These are shown when Protocol is SMTP.

Setting What it does Host The mail server's address, such as smtp.example.com. Port The mail server's port: 25, 587, 465, 2525, or other to type your own. Username The login for the mail server. Password The password for the mail server. It's stored in the settings table as plain text. Encryption None, TLS or SSL. Use what your provider asks for. Timeout How many seconds to wait for the mail server before giving up. Persistent connection Keeps the connection to the mail server open between emails. Helps when the site sends many emails at once.

docs.title: Meta Info
docs.text:
Bonfire provides Entity-Attribute-Value style storage for additional data of entities without modifying the underlying models and database tables. By default it can be used to add meta information to users, and it can be adapted to store meta information for the entities managed by your own admin modules.

We will explore an example of using Meta Info on users resource. For a short walkthrough, see Add a Custom Field to User Profiles.

By default, Bonfire comes with a pretty limited amount of data saved to a user. Most applications will likely require additional information available to the user, whether this is a bio, a website URL, the name of the school they attended, or anything else. Bonfire provides User Meta information that you can easily define to add additional information to a user. This data is seamlessly integrated into the Create/Edit User form so you do not have to modify that manually.

docs.title: Defining Meta Fields
docs.text:
All fields are defined within app/Config/Users.php. Two fields are provided (though commented out) as examples. Additionally, if you need labels for fields in validation messages, or if you need custom validation messages, expand the $metaFields 'validation' value into multidimensional array of it's own, with keys label and rules like it is done with 'baz' value below (in case of custom error messages, you can add them in errors subarray, see Validation in Codeigniter 4 documentation for more details).

public $metaFields = [
        'Example Fields' => [
            'foo' => ['label' => 'Foo', 'type' => 'text', 'validation' => 'permit_empty|string'],
            'Bar' => ['type' => 'text', 'validation' => 'required|string'],
            'baz' => [
                'label' => 'Baz',
                'type' => 'checkbox',
                'validation' => [
                    'label' => 'Baz',
                    'rules' => 'required|in_list[true,false]'
                ],
            ],
        ],
    ];

Each major grouping within the $metaFields array specifies a fieldset legend name. This provides logical grouping of fields within the Edit User form.

Each entry within this fieldset is a single piece of information. The key is the name that you would refer to the field by later. Then each has an array of information that defines it. The array has the following options that you can specify:

  • label is the label shown for the HTML input (if label is within validation sub-array, it is displayed in validation messages).

  • type is the type of HTML input. Currently most of the text-type inputs are supported (text, password, email, date, number, etc) as well as checkboxes, and textareas for when you need more information.

  • validation is the set of validation rules that should be applied to this field when saving, or a container for validation array of a field (with optional label, rules, errors keys).

docs.title: Using Meta Info
docs.text:
The User entity has a trait applied, HasMeta, that provides all the functionality you should need to work with the meta information for that user.

meta(string $key)

This returns the value of the user's meta named $key, or null if nothing has been set for that user. The name is the key of the array mentioned above.

$website = $user->meta('website_url');

allMeta()

This returns all meta fields for this user, indexed by meta key. Note that each entry is the full database row, not just the value.

$meta = $user->allMeta();

var_dump($meta['website_url']);

// Returns an object with:
    resource_id => 123
    class       => 'Bonfire\Users\User'
    key         => 'website_url'
    value       => 'https://example.com'
    created_at  => '2021-01-12 12:31:12'
    updated_at  => '2021-01-12 12:31:12'

allMetaKeyValue()

This returns all meta fields for this user as a simple array of key/value pairs.

$meta = $user->allMetaKeyValue();

// Returns:
[
    'website_url' => 'https://example.com',
]

hasMeta(string $key)

Used to check if a user has a value set for the given meta field.

if ($user->hasMeta('foo')) {
    //
}

saveMeta(string $key, $value)

Saves a single meta value to the user. This is immediately saved. There is no need to save the User through the UserModel.

$url = $this->request->getPost('website_url');
$user->saveMeta('website_url', $url);

deleteMeta(string $key)

Deletes a single meta value from the user. This is immediately deleted. There is no need to save the User through the UserModel.

$user->deleteMeta('website_url');

deleteResourceMeta()

Deletes all meta info associated with an entity. To be used when purging a record.

$user->deleteResourceMeta();

syncMeta(array $post)

Given an array of key/value pairs representing the name of the meta field and it's value, this will update existing meta values, insert new ones, and delete any that are passed in with an empty value. Only fields defined in the config file's $metaFields are saved; other keys are ignored. Useful when grabbing the information from a form and updating all the values at once.

$post = [
    'website_url' => 'https://example.com',
    'facebook_name' => 'johnny.rose'
];
$user->syncMeta($post);

syncMeta() will also delete meta data for the resource that is present in meta_info but not present in the corresponding config file's $metaFields property, and therefore not used (usually happens if you change $metaFields at some point, thus orphaning some data).

metaValidationRules(string $prefix=null)

This examines the specified config file and returns an array with the names of each field and their validation rules, ready to be used within CodeIgniter's validation library. If your form groups the name as an array, (like meta[website_url]) you may specify the prefix to append to the field names so that validation will pick it up properly.

$rules = $user->metaValidationRules('meta');

var_dump($rules);

// Returns:
[
    'meta.website_url' => 'required|string|valid_url',
]

docs.title: Using Meta on Your Classes
docs.text:
The meta solution is flexible enough to be used outside of Users in your own classes, if desired. There are two steps required to make that work.

  1. Create a Config file. This should include a $metaFields array, formatted as described above.
  2. Add the HasMeta trait and a protected $configClass property with a string value, the name of the above-mentioned Config class containing $metaFields array, to the Entity class that represents your resource.
use Bonfire\Core\Traits\HasMeta;
use CodeIgniter\Entity\Entity;

class CustomEntity extends Entity
{
    use HasMeta;

    protected string $configClass = 'CustomConfig';
}

docs.title: General Settings
docs.text:
The General settings screen holds the site's name, whether it's online, the admin's accent color, and how dates and times are shown. Open General under Settings in the sidebar. You need the admin.settings permission.

Change what you need, then click Save Settings.

docs.title: Take the site offline
docs.text:
To work on the site without visitors seeing it:

  1. Turn off Site Online.
  2. Click Save Settings.

While the site is offline, visitors are sent to an offline page. Members of the Super Admin group, and users with the site.viewOffline permission, can still use the whole site. Turn Site Online back on to open the site again.

A developer can change the offline page with Site::$siteOfflineView, see the Configuration Reference.

docs.title: Change the accent color
docs.text: The accent color is used for buttons, links and active items across the admin. Click one of the four preset swatches, or pick any color from the color picker. The admin previews the color as you pick; click Save Settings to keep it.

docs.title: General
docs.text: Setting What it does Site Name The site's name. It appears in the admin, and the rest of the site can use it. Required. Site Online When off, only Super Admins and users with site.viewOffline can reach the site.

docs.title: Appearance
docs.text: Setting What it does Accent Color The admin's highlight color, as a six-digit hex color like #2F6FEB.

docs.title: Date and Time
docs.text:
Setting What it does Timezone The site's timezone. Pick a region first, such as America or Europe, then a city. UTC needs no city. Date Format How dates are shown. Each choice shows today's date in that format: mm/dd/yyyy, dd/mm/yyyy, dd-mm-yyyy, yyyy-mm-dd, mmm dd, yyyy or dd.mm.yyyy. Time Format 12-hour (3:45 PM) or 24-hour (15:45).

The admin uses the date and time formats wherever it shows a date, such as the logs and a user's recent logins.

docs.title: Items per page
docs.text: How many rows admin lists show per page isn't set here. A developer sets it with Site::$perPage, 15 by default, or with setting('Site.perPage', 25). See the Configuration Reference.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text: The Tools module adds two screens under Tools in the sidebar: System Info, a summary of the server Bonfire runs on, and Logs, a viewer for the site's log files. It also adds three dashboard widgets: Log activity, Recent errors and System health.

docs.title: System Info
docs.text: Open System Info under Tools. You need the admin.settings permission.

docs.title: Server
docs.text: Item What it shows PHP Version The version of PHP running the site. CodeIgniter Version The version of CodeIgniter installed. SQL Engine The database driver and the database server's version. Server OS The server's operating system, release and architecture. Server Load The server's load average over the last minute, or Unknown where the server doesn't report it. Max Upload The largest file PHP accepts in an upload (upload_max_filesize). Max POST The largest form submission PHP accepts (post_max_size). Memory Limit The most memory one request may use (memory_limit).

docs.title: Filesystem
docs.text:
Bonfire writes logs, cache files and uploads to the /writable folder. This section shows:

  • whether a .env file is present. Missing is a warning, not an error: a site can be set up without one;
  • whether /writable and each file and folder in it can be written to, with the size and date of each file.

If anything there is Not writable, a warning appears at the top of the section. Ask whoever runs your server to let the web server write to that folder.

docs.title: Share your system details
docs.text:
When you report a bug, the details on this screen help others reproduce it:

  1. Click Copy as text. The button says Copied once the details are on your clipboard.
  2. Paste them into your bug report.

View PHP Info opens PHP's full configuration report in a new tab. It can hold paths and other details about your server, so check it before you share it.

docs.title: Logs
docs.text:
Open Logs under Tools. You need the logs.view permission to read logs, and logs.manage to delete them.

The site writes one log file per day to writable/logs. What gets logged is set in app/Config/Logger.php.

docs.title: The log list
docs.text:
The list shows one row per file, newest first: the date, a bar and tags counting the entries at each level, the total number of entries, and the file name.

Click With errors to show only files that have error, critical, alert or emergency entries, or With warnings for files with warnings. These chips filter the files on the current page.

docs.title: Read a log file
docs.text:
Click a date in the list. The file's entries are shown in the order they were logged, each with its level, time and message. Entries with a stack trace have a Stack trace line you can click to expand.

To find an entry:

  • choose a level: All, Errors (error, critical, alert and emergency), Warnings, Info (info and notice) or Debug;
  • type in Search messages to show only entries whose message contains your text.

Both filter the entries on the current page. The arrows at the top right move to the day before or after.

docs.title: Download a log file
docs.text: Open the file and click Download. You get the raw .log file, for example to attach to a bug report.

docs.title: Delete log files
docs.text:
You need the logs.manage permission. Deleted log files can't be restored.

  • One file: open it, click Delete log file and confirm.
  • Some files: tick them in the list, choose Delete from the bar at the bottom and confirm.
  • Every file: click Delete all log files above the list and confirm.

docs.title: Users
docs.text:
The Users module is where you add, edit, ban and delete the people who can log in to your site. Open it from Users under Content in the sidebar. You need the users.list permission to see it.

The rules for registration, logins, passwords and avatars live on a separate screen, Settings → Users.

docs.title: The user list
docs.text:
The list shows each user's avatar, name and email, username, groups, status and when they were last active. A user's status is one of:

  • Active: can log in.
  • Pending: has registered but hasn't confirmed their email address yet.
  • Banned: can't log in.

To narrow the list down:

  • type in the search box to match names, usernames and email addresses;
  • click a group chip to show only that group's members. Each chip shows how many users are in that group;
  • open the filter panel to filter by group, by whether a user is active or banned, or by when they were last active.

The list shows 15 users per page by default. There's no field for this in the admin; a developer sets it with Site::$perPage, see the Configuration Reference.

docs.title: Add a user
docs.text:
You need the users.create permission.

  1. Click New User above the list.
  2. Fill in the email address and username. First and last name are optional.
  3. Pick the user's groups, and upload an avatar if you like.
  4. Click Save User.

A user you add is active straight away. They get a random password, so either set one for them or ask them to use the "forgot password" link on the login page.

Note

Email addresses must be unique, and that includes users in the Recycler. If an address is "already in use" but you can't find the user, look in the Recycler under Tools.

docs.title: Edit a user
docs.text:
Click a user's name in the list. Their page has three tabs:

  • Details: profile, access and groups.
  • Permissions: permissions given to this user on top of their groups'. You need users.edit to see this tab.
  • Security: change the password and see recent logins.

Other modules can add tabs of their own.

You need users.edit to edit other users. Users with the me.edit permission can edit their own details, and those with me.security can change their own password.

docs.title: Upload or remove an avatar
docs.text:
On the Details tab, choose an image under the avatar, then click Save User. A new image replaces the old one. To remove an uploaded image, click Delete uploaded image and confirm.

Without an uploaded image, a user's avatar shows their initials, or their Gravatar if Gravatar is turned on.

docs.title: Activate a user
docs.text: A Pending user hasn't confirmed their email address. To let them in without it, turn on User is activated and click Save User. Once a user is active, you can't switch them back to pending.

docs.title: Ban a user
docs.text:
1. Turn on User is banned.
  2. Optionally, enter a reason. The user sees it when they try to log in.
  3. Click Save User.

To lift the ban, turn the switch off and save. You can't ban yourself, and only users with users.manage-admins can ban members of the Admin or Super Admin groups.

docs.title: Change a user's groups
docs.text:
Tick the groups the user belongs to, then click Save User. Each group card shows how many permissions the group grants.

Only users with users.manage-admins can add someone to the Admin or Super Admin groups, or take them out. For everyone else those groups are greyed out, and saving leaves them as they were.

docs.title: Give a user extra permissions
docs.text:
A user gets every permission of their groups. The Permissions tab adds permissions for this one user:

  1. Open the Permissions tab.
  2. Turn on the permissions to add. A permission the user already has through a group shows a lock and the group's name, like via admin. To take it away, change the user's groups.
  3. Click Save Permissions.

Only users with users.manage-admins can give someone a new users.* permission.

docs.title: Change a user's password
docs.text:
1. Open the Security tab.
  2. Enter the new password twice. The meter next to the field shows how strong it is.
  3. Click Update Password.

The password has to follow the rules under Passwords.

The Recent Logins table below shows the user's last 20 login attempts: when, from which IP address and browser, and whether they succeeded.

docs.title: Delete users
docs.text:
You need the users.delete permission.

  1. Tick the users in the list, or open the ⋯ menu on a user's row.
  2. Choose Delete and confirm.

You can't select yourself, and only users with users.manage-admins can delete users who manage admins.

Deleted users go to the Recycler under Tools, where you can restore them or delete them for good.

docs.title: Settings → Users
docs.text: Open Users under Settings in the sidebar. You need the users.settings permission. Click Save Settings when you're done.

docs.title: Registration
docs.text: Setting What it does Allow registration Lets people sign up on the site themselves. When off, only an admin can add users. Force email verification Emails new users a code to confirm their address. Until they do, they're Pending. Default user group The group people join when they sign up.

docs.title: Login
docs.text: Setting What it does Remember users Offers "remember me" at login, so users don't have to log in on every visit. Remember for How long "remember me" lasts, from 1 hour to 1 year. Shown when Remember users is on. Force 2FA after login Emails users a code to confirm each login.

docs.title: Passwords
docs.text:
Setting What it does Minimum length The fewest characters a password can have. At least 8; 10 is recommended. Composition Validator Checks the password's length requirements. Nothing Personal Validator Rejects passwords too similar to the user's email, username or other personal details. Dictionary Validator Rejects about 600,000 known leaked passwords, using a list on your server. Pwned Validator Rejects leaked passwords by asking haveibeenpwned.com.

The Dictionary and Pwned validators do the same job, so you only need one. Pwned has the bigger list but sends a partial hash of each new password to an outside service. With no validator on, a password only needs the minimum length.

docs.text: Setting What it does Initials from What avatar initials are made from when there's no image: Full Name (first and last initial, or the first two letters of the username if there's no first name) or Username (its first two letters). Use Gravatar Shows a user's Gravatar when they haven't uploaded an avatar. Gravatar default style The picture Gravatar shows for addresses without one, such as mystery person or identicon. Shown when Use Gravatar is on. Downsize on upload Shrinks uploaded avatars that are bigger than Max dimensions. Max dimensions The largest width or height of an uploaded avatar, in pixels. Shown when Downsize on upload is on. It can't be less than Users::$avatarResizeFloor, 32 by default.
